Oct 21 (Reuters) - A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history. The ruling came in a ‌case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their ‌consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the ​heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion. In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new ‌rules for what people can say online." New Mexico Attorney General Raúl ⁠Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history. Meta previously faced a $5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related ⁠to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health. New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users ​in ​New Mexico about who had access to their data and its handling of hate speech and misinformation posted ​on the platform. It alleged the company knew third parties had broad ‌access to users' data and tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line. Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers." Mathew's decision comes as Meta faces thousands of lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers over the impact of Instagram and Facebook on teen mental health, with another trial slated to begin next week. Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942 million in a pair of trials against Meta over ‌claims it facilitated sexual exploitation of young people on Instagram and Facebook and misled consumers about the ​platforms' safety. Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the latest New Mexico ruling costly ​but unlikely to impact the company's value. "Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and ​will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said. Jurors in September had found that the company and ‌its leadership made 26 misleading statements on data privacy, hate speech and ​other subjects. Multiplying those statements by their potential ​audience, they said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws. At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion. "This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the ​value of its stock price," McGinn said. In court filings, Meta urged ‌Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had ​actually been misled, the company said in court filings. (Reporting by Diana Novak Jones in Chicago, additional reporting by Andrew Hay in New Mexico and Jaspreet Singh ​and Anzar Mehraj in Bangalore. Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Nia Williams, Aurora Ellis and Stephen Coates)

Oct 21 (Reuters) - A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.

The ruling came in a ‌case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their ‌consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.

"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the ​heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new ‌rules for what people can say online."
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl ⁠Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.
Meta previously faced a $5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related ⁠to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health.
New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users ​in ​New Mexico about who had access to their data and its handling of hate speech and misinformation posted ​on the platform. It alleged the company knew third parties had broad ‌access to users' data and tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line.
Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting.

"It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers."
Mathew's decision comes as Meta faces thousands of lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers over the impact of Instagram and Facebook on teen mental health, with another trial slated to begin next week.

Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942 million in a pair of trials against Meta over ‌claims it facilitated sexual exploitation of young people on Instagram and Facebook and misled consumers about the ​platforms' safety.
Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the latest New Mexico ruling costly ​but unlikely to impact the company's value.
"Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and ​will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said.

Jurors in September had found that the company and ‌its leadership made 26 misleading statements on data privacy, hate speech and ​other subjects. Multiplying those statements by their potential ​audience, they said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws.
At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion.
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the ​value of its stock price," McGinn said.

In court filings, Meta urged ‌Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had ​actually been misled, the company said in court filings.

(Reporting by Diana Novak Jones in Chicago, additional reporting by Andrew Hay in New Mexico and Jaspreet Singh ​and Anzar Mehraj in Bangalore. Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Nia Williams, Aurora Ellis and Stephen Coates)

Meta was ordered to pay New Mexico a $25 billion civil penalty in the Cambridge Analytica Facebook case after a jury found the company liable for more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws.

Judge Francis Mathew issued the order in Santa Fe, and the ruling came after jurors found Meta violated New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act based on widely viewed deceptive statements about how it handled hate speech and user data.
Judge found a willfully ineffective internal investigation

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez called the judgment “one of the single largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against the company in American history,” and he said the payment would be put toward public education in the state.

Judge Francis Mathew wrote that “Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” and the ruling said the deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked.

Meta said the ruling and Torrez’s office’s approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” and Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said it was “confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws tied to Cambridge Analytica harvesting Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season. The case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. Judge Francis Mathew said the penalty was supported by “the extraordinary number of deliberate violations found by the jury,” and he cited the involvement of high-ranking Facebook executives and the “clear intentional and systematic nature” of the repeated false statements.

New Mexico sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, and Meta’s lawyers argued for paying no more than $3.4 billion, with Meta saying an award many times larger would be unconstitutional. Meta also argued that the state failed to prove misleading statements and that content moderation actually harmed people in New Mexico, while New Mexico prosecutors argued the company’s statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users.

The ruling set interest to accrue on the penalty at an annual rate of 15% until Meta fully paid the fine, and the judge justified the sanction under New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act. New Mexico officials said the fines would go toward education spending, and Torrez said the state intended “to do everything in our power to make sure that those resources are eventually delivered” to New Mexico. Meta said it planned to appeal, and the company argued that interest would accrue during an appeal while the number of violations could be reduced.

The Cambridge Analytica penalty also arrived as Meta continued to invest in artificial intelligence, with the company launching its Muse AI personal assistant app in September and reporting that its AI investments were boosting its core advertising business. Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project, said $25 billion is “a drop in the bucket for Meta,” and she added that “Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information.”

Oct 21 (Reuters) - A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history. The ruling came in a ‌case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their ‌consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the ​heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion. In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new ‌rules for what people can say online." New Mexico Attorney General Raúl ⁠Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history. Meta previously faced a $5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related ⁠to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health. New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users ​in ​New Mexico about who had access to their data and its handling of hate speech and misinformation posted ​on the platform. It alleged the company knew third parties had broad ‌access to users' data and tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line. Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers." Mathew's decision comes as Meta faces thousands of lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers over the impact of Instagram and Facebook on teen mental health, with another trial slated to begin next week. Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942 million in a pair of trials against Meta over ‌claims it facilitated sexual exploitation of young people on Instagram and Facebook and misled consumers about the ​platforms' safety. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.

"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the ​heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new ‌rules for what people can say online."

Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting.

"I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers."

Meta was ordered to pay New Mexico a $25 billion civil penalty in the Cambridge Analytica Facebook case after a jury found the company liable for more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws.

Judge Francis Mathew issued the order in Santa Fe, and the ruling came after jurors found Meta violated New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act based on widely viewed deceptive statements about how it handled hate speech and user data.
Judge found a willfully ineffective internal investigation

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez called the judgment “one of the single largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against the company in American history,” and he said the payment would be put toward public education in the state.

Judge Francis Mathew wrote that “Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” and the ruling said the deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked.

Meta said the ruling and Torrez’s office’s approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” and Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said it was “confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws tied to Cambridge Analytica harvesting Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season. The case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. Judge Francis Mathew said the penalty was supported by “the extraordinary number of deliberate violations found by the jury,” and he cited the involvement of high-ranking Facebook executives and the “clear intentional and systematic nature” of the repeated false statements.

New Mexico sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, and Meta’s lawyers argued for paying no more than $3.4 billion, with Meta saying an award many times larger would be unconstitutional. Meta also argued that the state failed to prove misleading statements and that content moderation actually harmed people in New Mexico, while New Mexico prosecutors argued the company’s statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users.

The ruling set interest to accrue on the penalty at an annual rate of 15% until Meta fully paid the fine, and the judge justified the sanction under New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act. New Mexico officials said the fines would go toward education spending, and Torrez said the state intended “to do everything in our power to make sure that those resources are eventually delivered” to New Mexico. Meta said it planned to appeal, and the company argued that interest would accrue during an appeal while the number of violations could be reduced.

The Cambridge Analytica penalty also arrived as Meta continued to invest in artificial intelligence, with the company launching its Muse AI personal assistant app in September and reporting that its AI investments were boosting its core advertising business. Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project, said $25 billion is “a drop in the bucket for Meta,” and she added that “Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information.”

relevantPassages.text: A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the ​company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.
New Mexico’s attorney general sued Meta ​in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.
Meta previously faced a $5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, ​but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
In court ​filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion.

Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states’ claims that the company’s platforms had harmed teen mental health.
Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A.
“Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out,” Luria said.
“This court should ⁠speak to Meta ​in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said.
Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on ⁠appeal.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge ​Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.

It added there were further "exploitation attempts" once the embargo on the flaw warning was lifted. The company said it "automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability." When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web. Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites. As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like." Why have websites around the world been taken down? He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI". Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October. In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said. The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said. extraction.body: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks. According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation , composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity". A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet. Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected. Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found". Wiz wrote in a blog post about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites. The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker". Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts. Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale. The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post. The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure. "Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre. The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users - meaning most people won't need to take any action. Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes - known as patching - is "a bit like running a Windows update". If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied - something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins. If you look after your website yourself, Munro says "it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied". "Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said . And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

passages: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.
It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.
The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.
Cyber-security firm Wiz – one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities – described the flaws as the “most severe” ever detected by AI.
OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory”.
It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.
According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world’s websites.
It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation, composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its “long-term prosperity”.
A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet.
Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined “php2shell” – were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected.
Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was “the most serious vulnerability I’ve ever found”.

Wiz wrote in a blog post about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data – saying everything built on PHP was left exposed.
AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.
He estimated the flaw could affect “millions and millions” of websites.
Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be “disastrous” if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites.
The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.
That includes Wikimedia – the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia – which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.
Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands’ cyber-security agency also pulling its website.
A number of Scotland’s public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.
Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.
More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.
The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.
“These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies,” the agency said.
The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”.
Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.
Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform’s developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.
The incident “highlights how AI can uncover security flaws” but also how it can “help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” OpenAI said in a blog post.
The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure.

“Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind,” said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland’s Cyber Research Centre.
The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users – meaning most people won’t need to take any action.
Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes – known as patching – is “a bit like running a Windows update”.

If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied – something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins.
If you look after your website yourself, Munro says “it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied”.
“Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount,” it said.
And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a statement. , external Amazon said its threat intelligence system identified it was targeted on Saturday. It added there were further "exploitation attempts" once the embargo on the flaw warning was lifted. The company said it "automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability." When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web. Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites. As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like." Why have websites around the world been taken down? BBC explains Cyber security researcher Ryan Austin, who has been researching PHP security for the last 20 years, said he discovered the flaw in the programming language. He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI". Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October. In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said. The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said. In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said. The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning. It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. extraction.body: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks. According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation , composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity". A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet. Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected. Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found". Wiz wrote in a blog post about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites. The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker". Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts. Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale. The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post. The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure. "Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre. The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users - meaning most people won't need to take any action. Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes - known as patching - is "a bit like running a Windows update". If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied - something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins. If you look after your website yourself, Munro says "it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied". "Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said . And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation, composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its “long-term prosperity”.
A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet.
Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined “php2shell” – were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected.
Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was “the most serious vulnerability I’ve ever found”.

Wiz wrote in a blog post about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data – saying everything built on PHP was left exposed.
AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.
He estimated the flaw could affect “millions and millions” of websites.
Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be “disastrous” if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites.
The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.
That includes Wikimedia – the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia – which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.
Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands’ cyber-security agency also pulling its website.
A number of Scotland’s public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.
Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.
More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.
The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.
“These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies,” the agency said.
The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”.
Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.
Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform’s developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.
The incident “highlights how AI can uncover security flaws” but also how it can “help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” OpenAI said in a blog post.
The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure.

“Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind,” said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland’s Cyber Research Centre.
The issue affects back-end website and web development processes that will be invisible to many users – meaning most people won’t need to take any action.
Ethical hacker Ken Munro, who has spent years finding security flaws in computer systems, says installing the fixes – known as patching – is “a bit like running a Windows update”.

If a hosting company or web developer manages your website, contact them and ask whether the PHP security fixes have been applied – something that must be applied to PHP itself and cannot be resolved by updating WordPress or its plugins.
If you look after your website yourself, Munro says “it is your own responsibility to make sure fixes are applied”.
“Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount,” it said.
And while the onus lies mainly on website operators, users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

extraction.body: In today’s market, no single metric defines what a Series A is, or how to raise one. At this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt, three investors offered founders advice on raising one, and one of them tacked on a warning. With money pouring into AI and revenue numbers being inflated to justify sky-high valuations, a correction could come as soon as 2027. The warning came from Shailendra Singh, a managing director at Peak XV, who spoke alongside Jahanvi Sardana, a partner at Index Ventures, and Jenelle Teng Wade, a partner at Bessemer. “Seed and venture, I’ve never seen it as dysfunctional as it is now,” Singh said, adding that the current market is one of the hardest to raise in that he has seen. “The burden is high to convince any top firm that you are amongst the few special companies that can break out, and then the dispersion is very high on the terms you might get, how much capital you can raise, and what terms you can raise it,” he continued. In fact, it’s common now to see a company trying to close a round with as many as three different prices at once. “[I]’s a crazy sign of market froth,” he said. “We’re calling it the ‘tranchopalooza,’” Sardana added, referring to the way rounds are being split into tranches, or separate chunks. Beyond the warnings, the investors laid out what they look for in a Series A pitch, including, first, a persuasive story about why a founder has a shot at building a big company. “Founders who can attract very high-quality talent have an advantage,” Singh added. What a founder builds matters, too. Teng Wade said capital is flowing into areas such as defense, robotics, and AI infrastructure. She also noted that foundational model companies are moving toward vertical integration (taking on more of the stack themselves), but there’s still room for newer players, including neo-clouds that rent out AI computing power and neo-labs focused on AI research. Metrics, meanwhile, still help a lot, but they are less defined than they used to be, especially in an era like AI where it’s incredibly expensive to run a company. Teng Wade gave an example of how her firm evaluated Anthropic in its early days, when its margins were negative, and it was spending heavily on compute. One partner on her team, however, felt that AI was going to be “bigger than everything we’ve ever expected in terms of price premium on the frontier models,” she said, “becoming a substitute for other types of software.” The logic was that even with money-losing margins, the market would be big enough to pay off if the company became one of the top three players. Anthropic is now reportedly preparing an IPO at a valuation of around $2 trillion . It told investors this month it was profitable on an adjusted basis , though that measure excludes some costs. The investors also spoke about the importance of honesty in a market like this, where inflated annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers are swirling alongside headline valuations. “I tell founders, If you ever show a chart which shows cumulative revenue or cumulative ARR, that is a massive red flag,” Singh said. “It means that your time series data is not good because cumulative data is a big lie.” Added Singh: It’s important for a company to be intellectually honest in how they are presenting and engaging in bull cycles.” Singh said the market is full of “false positives” because “it can’t be that every company is going to be successful. This is as optimistic as I’ve seen the venture world in two decades, and normally it’s a sign. I think 2027 will be different. I think we will see a correction.” Finally, the panelists were asked to give founders at least one piece of parting advice. Singh went first, reminding founders that building a company is one of the “most excruciatingly difficult things” one can do. And with that, “deal with it,” he said. He also urged founders not to rush into something, to watch out for weak product-market fit, and always hold the bar very high for what they are trying to solve. Sardana said it is important to know how to pitch but that founders should be careful not to let that dictate what they build. “It feels like [founders are] deciding what to build based on what’s getting funded, which is really scary,” she continued. Teng Wade, meanwhile, said her typical advice of telling founders to be conservative with their projections and requests hasn’t really held up. “I would say just be audacious in your ask,” she now says, and see how the market responds, “and then you can tailor from there.” Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings Anthony Ha Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says Kirsten Korosec Lucas Ropek Rebecca Bellan Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept Connie Loizos

sources.title: Your Investors Can Make Or Break Your Startup. Here’s Who Founders Actually Need On Their Cap Table - Crunchbase News
passages: Here’s what founders should look for in their investors.
In those moments, founders need someone they can call before they have the polished explanation prepared.
Which is why founders should have at least one investor who “gets” them, not simply their market or business model, but how they operate as a person.
Every founder has heard that investors should bring more than money.
If I were a founder building a venture-backed company, I would ask myself of every potential investor: What can they materially help this company accomplish over the next 18 to 24 months?

Investors actively evaluating companies at a particular stage can add another layer of qualitative context: what the market is rewarding right now, how expectations are shifting, and which milestones founders should prioritize before their next raise.
Crunchbase News spoke with James Kim, partner at Reach Capital, about how Reach’s education roots inform its broader strategy, what it saw in AI...
The strongest cap tables are intentionally constructed around investors who bring different forms of value.
The most overlooked investor may also be the most important: someone the founder actually trusts.
As startups mature, some investors may ultimately gain board seats and significant influence over decisions ranging from fundraising and acquisitions to leadership changes.
Founders therefore shouldn’t simply ask investors about their portfolio.
By Series A, investors may expect evidence that the company can scale what is already working.
As an early-stage investor, I always advise entrepreneurs to recognize that you’re not simply raising money, you’re also deciding who will sit at the table you’re building.
Founders have to seek out strategic investors: People or institutions with industry expertise, relationships and resources that can help founders solve problems capital alone cannot.
That relationship can be especially consequential for founders navigating rooms where few investors share their background or experiences.
A trusted investor can help interpret dynamics, prepare for difficult conversations, and provide candid advice without making every mistake feel like an indictment of the founder’s ability to lead.

extraction.body: For founders raising venture capital, the instinct is often to get the money, as much and as quickly as possible. And it’s no secret that fundraising can be grueling, especially after dozens of pitches, follow-ups and rejections. It can almost feel as though a term sheet is the validation and that the hardest part is finally over. But founders also have to pay attention to far more than the size of the check or the valuation attached to it. They should be asking a much bigger question: Who exactly am I allowing onto my cap table and to own a piece of my company? Venture capital isn’t a loan. Investors receive ownership in the company in exchange for the money they put in. As startups mature, some investors may ultimately gain board seats and significant influence over decisions ranging from fundraising and acquisitions to leadership changes. As an early-stage investor, I always advise entrepreneurs to recognize that you’re not simply raising money, you’re also deciding who will sit at the table you’re building. That means the goal shouldn’t be assembling a cap table filled with whoever was willing to invest. The strongest cap tables are intentionally constructed around investors who bring different forms of value. Here’s what founders should look for in their investors. Every founder has heard that investors should bring more than money. The phrase has become such a fundraising cliché that it can lose its meaning. If I were a founder building a venture-backed company, I would ask myself of every potential investor: What can they materially help this company accomplish over the next 18 to 24 months? For a fintech founder, the answer might be introductions to banks, regulators, payment companies or potential enterprise customers. A healthcare investor might provide access to hospital systems, insurers, or executives who understand lengthy procurement cycles. An investor in consumer products may understand distribution, retail partnerships, or customer acquisition. Founders have to seek out strategic investors: People or institutions with industry expertise, relationships and resources that can help founders solve problems capital alone cannot. This becomes particularly important when something goes wrong. When growth stalls, a key hire leaves or a partnership disappears, the investor who can introduce five potential customers on Monday is significantly more useful than one whose primary contribution was wiring money six months earlier. Founders therefore shouldn’t simply ask investors about their portfolio. They should conduct the due diligence in the same way that investors diligence them. Ask what their platform support typically entails. Talk to portfolio founders. Find out whether the investor was useful when the company struggled. Reputation and access should be proven, not promised. A billion-dollar growth investor may have an impressive résumé. That doesn’t necessarily mean they understand how to help a company with six employees, an unfinished product, and nine months of runway. Startup problems change dramatically by stage. For example, at pre-seed, founders may still be validating the market and searching for product-market fit. At seed, the challenge might become hiring, repeatability and proving customers will consistently pay. By Series A, investors may expect evidence that the company can scale what is already working. That makes stage-specific investors particularly valuable. Investors who repeatedly work with companies at the same point in their development have seen the movie before. They know what metrics the next round of investors will examine, which mistakes frequently derail companies, and what milestones founders should prioritize before returning to market. They also have something founders won’t necessarily find in a database: current fundraising intelligence. Forward-looking business intelligence can complement that firsthand perspective. A platform like Crunchbase combines data on past financings with predictions and insights designed to surface company momentum and likely future developments. Investors actively evaluating companies at a particular stage can add another layer of qualitative context: what the market is rewarding right now, how expectations are shifting, and which milestones founders should prioritize before their next raise. The best investor isn’t necessarily the person with the biggest fund. Sometimes it is the person who knows exactly what your company needs to look like 12 months from now. The most overlooked investor may also be the most important: someone the founder actually trusts. Startups inevitably encounter moments when things go wrong. Revenue misses projections. Co-founders disagree. Executives quit. Products fail. Fundraising takes longer than expected. In those moments, founders need someone they can call before they have the polished explanation prepared. Which is why founders should have at least one investor who “gets” them, not simply their market or business model, but how they operate as a person. That relationship can be especially consequential for founders navigating rooms where few investors share their background or experiences. A trusted investor can help interpret dynamics, prepare for difficult conversations, and provide candid advice without making every mistake feel like an indictment of the founder’s ability to lead. Founders should pay attention to how investors behave during fundraising because those interactions offer clues about what the relationship could become. Do they listen? Do they respect your judgment? Can they disagree without becoming dismissive? Do portfolio founders call them when things are going badly, or only when there is good news to report? Capital can help build a company. The wrong capital can make building it substantially harder. Before closing a round, founders should look beyond valuation and ask whether their cap table has all three forms of support: someone who knows the industry, someone who understands the stage and someone they genuinely trust. Because the most important decision in fundraising may not be how much money you raise. It may be who you allow to come along for the ride. extraction.body: On October 2, 2025, the National Venture Capital Association (NVCA) released it’s most recent updates to its model legal documents to reflect recent legal developments, market practices and regulatory priorities. The NVCA model legal documents (the “NVCA Docs”) remain the industry benchmark for venture financings in the U.S and have only become ubiquitous over the last five years in financing transactions – where they are commonly the starting point or benchmark for Company financing documents in such transactions. Due to such widespread adoption, any updates to such documents can carry significant ramifications for start-up companies and VC investors alike. The most recent updates refresh the NVCA agreements to reflect an evolving regulatory environment, investing principles and landscape, and introduce new alternatives and key updates, including around tranched financings, national security compliance, and corporate governance. For founders and investors, the practical takeaway is that these changes are designed to make diligence faster, representations more accurate and re-allocate risk where there is heightened uncertainty. Below, we unpack three areas that founders and investors should be aware of. 1. Tranched Financings Get a Formal Introduction (Stock Purchase Agreement) First, milestone-based or “tranched” financings are now formally addressed in the Stock Purchase Agreement (SPA) as an option where appropriate, and the NVCA updates include language for companies and investors to consider when the terms of the transaction call for implementing a tranched financing. A tranched financing is a venture round that is split into multiple closings, each contingent on the company achieving specific milestones. For example, rather than wiring the entire $10 million for a Series A financing upfront, an investor might instead: Tranched financing structures are not a new development, they have been employed in certain instances, including when appropriate to help manage elevated risk – such as risks tied to market uncertainty or heightened risks related to execution or achievement of a Company’s business plan. Tranched structures also allow investors to deploy money at a “just-in-time” basis, as milestones are often tied to the Company’s cash needs in accordance with its business plan, while also creating additional risk for the Company that an investor may or may not invest in accordance with its trance. Until the most recent updates, a tranched structure was not supported in the standard NVCA SPA. Now, companies and investors can use Annex to the SPA as a framework to define what “milestones” a company must achieve before a subsequent tranche closing is to take place. This aligns certain incentives but materially raises the stakes for investors who commit to staged funding and the company’s who are executing in reliance of those additional stages of funding. Given the evolution of market conditions, anecdotally, we can share that we are seeing tranche mechanics migrate from later-stage life sciences (where tranches commonly track stages of regulatory approval of drugs and other treatments) into earlier-stage “tech” transactions, particularly where go-to-market or regulatory risk is significant. Unfortunately this invariably comes with an increase in disputes in these same structures. Tranche-based investing can align capital with progress, but it also increases the surface area for disputes, and the potential for significant issues if those disputes lead to cash uncertainty. For that reason, it is imperative that investors and companies engage early with their advisors to define milestones, investment timing and dispute resolution procedures if the parties elect a tranche-based investing approach. Examples of such concerns include: How is a milestone and “achievement” of that milestone defined? For example, might the investor and company have a different definition of ARR? Or, if the milestones are based on an operational milestone such as launching a “version 2.0” product or signing a certain number of enterprise clients, who ultimately makes the call on whether these milestones have been achieved? What happens where investor approvals and controls prevent the achievement of a milestone? What happens if Investor cannot meet its later tranche obligations? Investors will need to consider whether they will be penalized if they fail to fund a required tranche. The model SPA now contains optional language that would convert the investor’s preferred stock into common stock of the company upon the investor’s failure to fund. This conversion would strip away an investor’s liquidation preference, anti-dilution, and other protective rights from previously purchased shares. Does the investor then need to consider segmenting such funds separately from the rest of its investment vehicle? Does the Company need further information to confirm the Investor will be in a position to fund? Tranche financing has appropriate uses, but where it is adopted it will be a significant change from standard financing approach and given the potential for uncertainty and conflict – founders will need to clearly define who determines milestone achievement (board, stockholders, or both) and ensure that the conditions are sufficiently objective and attainable and should model their cash runway with and without subsequent tranches; build fallbacks if a tranche is delayed; and ensure disclosure does not over-promise milestone feasibility. Investors will need to understand the risk of losing preferred rights in a tranched financing and confirm internal liquidity planning and side letter flexibility to ensure tranche obligations can be met without breaching fund concentration or borrowing limits. Both sides should work with their trusted advisors to document milestones thoughtfully to objective, auditable criteria, and include approval mechanics early to prevent future disputes which, if not quickly resolved, can lead to gridlock and ultimately, corporate failure. 2. Regulatory Compliance Takes Center Stage (Stock Purchase Agreement) Second, the updated SPA introduces new representations and warranties reflecting heightened U.S. national security and data security oversight. These provisions extend beyond traditional export controls and sanctions and, importantly, apply two‑ways—both to the company and to each purchaser. Two‑way representations matter because regulatory exposure often travels in both directions. For founders, an investor with undisclosed foreign beneficial ownership or control could jeopardize customer contracts, federal grants, or exit timing. For investors, a company’s unrecognized DSP status or OISP‑implicated activities could introduce enforcement risk, limit follow‑on financing options, or cause the investor unnecessary scrutiny across its portfolio. Reciprocal representations encourage both parties to actively consider the data and national security concerns up front, and support faster closings by allowing counsel to diligence to a common standard. From a negotiation standpoint, two‑way reps also encourage early disclosure and constructive problem‑solving—if either party anticipates a limitation, it can be resolved through disclosure schedules, targeted covenants, or sometimes through more complex deal designs (for example, SPV structuring, data segregation, or remediation timelines). A. Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) Effective January 2, 2025, final regulations under the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) implemented an Executive Order from the White House limiting or requiring notification of certain “covered transactions” by U.S. persons involving “covered foreign persons,” with particular focus on activities in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum computing linked to countries of concern, including China (and other specified territories such as Hong Kong and Macau). Following implementation of these regulations, the updated SPA includes representations and warranties requiring companies engaged in a VC financing to confirm that they: Effective April 8, 2025, the Data Security Program (DSP) imposes new restrictions on foreign-connected entities’ ability to access or process certain categories of U.S. government-related data or bulk personal data, including genomic, biometric, geolocation, and sensitive health information. To align with this framework, the updated SPA adds new representations and warranties from the company and each purchaser confirming that no party is a “covered person” under the DSP. Specifically, the parties must now represent that they are not: Companies and investors must now understand how their data flows, third-party vendors, and ownership structures intersect with these DSP regulated activities. For example, Companies handling health, mobility, or biometrics data must map data flows, vendors, and compute locations and investors with international LPs or co‑investment SPVs should test whether any beneficial ownership, control, or service provider relationships could inadvertently trip DSP definitions. C. Purchaser Representation — “Not a Person of Concern” The most recent NVCA update also introduces a two-way compliance obligation that applies to the company and investors. Investors (and not just companies) must now represent that they are not “persons of concern” under either the OISP or DSP regimes. This addition reflects the growing focus on the capital-flow side of national security – and therefore the acknowledgement that managing important technology and data cannot be wholly achieved by focusing only on the owners an distributors of the same, but also the investors who have financially supported those who hold such technology and data.. Practically, this means that even if a U.S. venture fund is an exempt reporting adviser, they should nonetheless review: For cross-border investors or funds with international LPs, this new clause may require legal opinions or disclosure schedules to confirm compliance. D. Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) Update 3. Adopting NVCA Corporate Governance Policies (Investors’ Rights Agreement) The NVCA’s updated Investors’ Rights Agreement (IRA) now encourages adoption of the NVCA’s governance policy suite, including HR and EEO frameworks, DEI initiatives, anti-harassment and whistleblower programs, and talent attraction and retention strategies. While not mandatory, these policies’ presence in the NVCA documents may cause them to become an expectation among institutional investors and can be a selling point in later-stage financing or exits, especially with institutional investors. Companies and investors should consider whether adopting these policies could streamline portfolio compliance, recruiting, and later‑stage due diligence. Many of the policies have a beneficial effect on the Company’s compliance culture but policies are restrictive in their nature and so should be adopted with an understanding of the restrictions and consequences for failure to abide by them. Adopting a form policy without a good understanding of how it may affect your business can lead to significant repercussions down the road. 4. Practical Guidance for Companies: Conduct a “Regulatory Health Check” Before Fundraising 5. Practical Guidance for Investors: Update Diligence, IC Memos, and LP Communications The NVCA changes should trigger immediate updates to form term sheets, diligence checklists, investment committee templates, and LP communications—particularly around OISP/DSP. Consider the following actions: Review your form term sheet: Many serial investors do not update their form term sheets as often as the NVCA documents are updated. If you have not done so recently it is time to work with your counsel and your team to update your form term sheet. Diligence Checklist Refresh. Insert targeted questions on OISP/DSP, including covered activities, foreign person links, data categories, compute locations, and government‑customer exposure. Request data‑flow diagrams and vendor inventories for DSP‑relevant sectors. Add QSBS confirmation requests, including gross‑assets history and redemption logs. The October 2025 NVCA updates are a pragmatic response to the “new normal” of national security oversight, data sensitivity, and capital‑flow scrutiny. They are not meant to chill investment; they are meant to clarify expectations and streamline execution. For founders and funds alike, proactively addressing these new requirements will close deals efficiently and avoid costly surprises.

sources.title: Founders and investors beware: Cram-down rounds for startups are coming
passages: Though they occur in any market, cram downs usually become much more common during downturns, when companies are forced to raise money at successively lower valuations, also known as "down rounds." For years, the VC industry seemed to defy gravity: Money poured into the sector, valuations soared, and it felt like there would always be a willing buyer to step in and bankroll a growing startup.
Jones said he's seeing more of what he calls "rescue rounds," in which a founder has to choose between a cram down and going out of business.
The investors that step up to fill that void — usually late-stage VC growth funds or strategic investors — often demand terms that severely dilute or "cram down" the shares of existing shareholders.

"It can be very painful," he said, "and there's many, many thousands of companies that are either gonna go under or are gonna be cramming down investors." Hirsch says the current moment reminds him of the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000, when cram downs became commonplace.

"That's where the knives tend to come out," said Hirsch, adding that cram-down negotiations can become highly contentious and rife with bitterness and brinksmanship as everyone moves to defend their interests.
Early investors in a company often retain what are known as pro rata rights — the right to buy into future funding rounds in order to maintain their share of the company.

Today, with the market in a tailspin, many investors are choosing not to participate in follow-on rounds, either because they can't come up with the money or because they don't want to take further risks on a struggling company.
He believes this will allow the company to avoid a painful down round.

extraction.body: Last summer, as valuations were soaring to record highs and venture capitalists were falling over themselves to throw money at startups, there was at least one person who was feeling pessimistic. Brian Hirsch, the founder and managing partner of Tribeca Venture Partners, said his firm made only one investment between January of 2020 and the third quarter of 2021. Having been in the VC game for more than 25 years, he knows what inevitably follows periods of irrational exuberance: cram downs. A cram-down round refers to a situation in which a company raises money at terms favorable to new investors, at the expense of current shareholders. Though they occur in any market, cram downs usually become much more common during downturns, when companies are forced to raise money at successively lower valuations, also known as "down rounds." For years, the VC industry seemed to defy gravity: Money poured into the sector, valuations soared, and it felt like there would always be a willing buyer to step in and bankroll a growing startup. Today, with private-market valuations plummeting, the IPO market on life support, and the macroeconomic environment looking shaky at best, many VCs have pulled back on deploying capital. Early investors in a company often retain what are known as pro rata rights — the right to buy into future funding rounds in order to maintain their share of the company. In good times, when valuations are going up and VCs have money to spare, exercising pro rata rights is usually a no-brainer. Today, with the market in a tailspin, many investors are choosing not to participate in follow-on rounds, either because they can't come up with the money or because they don't want to take further risks on a struggling company. The investors that step up to fill that void — usually late-stage VC growth funds or strategic investors — often demand terms that severely dilute or "cram down" the shares of existing shareholders. A shareholder who owns 20% of a company might get crammed down to 5%. They may also lose what are known as liquidation preferences, or the right to be paid first if the company is sold. For those investors who don't want to go along with these onerous terms, cram downs often include "pay-to-play" provisions, meaning those who either can't or won't provide additional capital can see their share of the company diluted to nothing. It essentially forces shareholders to pony up cash or be wiped out. "That's where the knives tend to come out," said Hirsch, adding that cram-down negotiations can become highly contentious and rife with bitterness and brinksmanship as everyone moves to defend their interests. Often employees and the investors who took an early chance are pitted against what they view as deep-pocketed interlopers gunning for a spot at the top of the cap table. "It can be very painful," he said, "and there's many, many thousands of companies that are either gonna go under or are gonna be cramming down investors." Hirsch says the current moment reminds him of the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000, when cram downs became commonplace. For many in the VC industry today who have only known boom times, the coming wave of these rounds may be a rude awakening. "There's a lot of people in our industry that are clueless and they're gonna need to get up to speed, quickly," said Hirsh. None more so than startup founders, who often stand to lose the most in a cram down. They usually don't have the thousands or even millions of dollars required to avoid being diluted down to nothing. "It's definitely a buyer's market, investors can kind of write whatever they want," said Michael Jones, the managing director of the venture firm Science Inc., which has invested in companies such as Liquid Death and Dollar Shave Club. Jones said he's seeing more of what he calls "rescue rounds," in which a founder has to choose between a cram down and going out of business. "Sometimes what happens obviously is the founder is just desperate and they just kind of sign whatever comes across their desk because they're worried about making payroll," he says. His advice to founders in the current environment: If you can avoid raising money, you should. Guy, the cofounder and CEO of the startup Sevco Security, said he's been approached by investors bearing so-called "dirty term sheets" containing cram down and pay-to-play provisions. "I've got a lot of folks, I'll say sharks circling in the water," he said. Lucky for him, Sevco is well capitalized at the moment and won't be needing to raise money anytime soon. What's more, he said he decided not to chase sky-high valuations during the boom, choosing instead to focus on customer relationships and revenue. He believes this will allow the company to avoid a painful down round. "Over the course the last 10 years, the consensus opinion was drive harder, drive faster, raise more capital, increase valuations, and that's what we as an industry celebrated," he said. "But that doesn't do anything except feed egos and the unrealized return metric on investor pitch decks."
