On October 2, 2025, the National Venture Capital Association (NVCA) released it’s most recent updates to its model legal documents to reflect recent legal developments, market practices and regulatory priorities.
Due to such widespread adoption, any updates to such documents can carry significant ramifications for start-up companies and VC investors alike.
The October 2025 NVCA updates are a pragmatic response to the “new normal” of national security oversight, data sensitivity, and capital‑flow scrutiny.
They are not meant to chill investment; they are meant to clarify expectations and streamline execution.
For founders and funds alike, proactively addressing these new requirements will close deals efficiently and avoid costly surprises.

Effective January 2, 2025, final regulations under the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) implemented an Executive Order from the White House limiting or requiring notification of certain “covered transactions” by U.S. persons involving “covered foreign persons,” with particular focus on activities in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum computing linked to countries of concern, including China (and other specified territories such as Hong Kong and Macau).
The most recent NVCA update also introduces a two-way compliance obligation that applies to the company and investors.

While not mandatory, these policies’ presence in the NVCA documents may cause them to become an expectation among institutional investors and can be a selling point in later-stage financing or exits, especially with institutional investors.

First, milestone-based or “tranched” financings are now formally addressed in the Stock Purchase Agreement (SPA) as an option where appropriate, and the NVCA updates include language for companies and investors to consider when the terms of the transaction call for implementing a tranched financing.

Tranche financing has appropriate uses, but where it is adopted it will be a significant change from standard financing approach and given the potential for uncertainty and conflict – founders will need to clearly define who determines milestone achievement (board, stockholders, or both) and ensure that the conditions are sufficiently objective and attainable and should model their cash runway with and without subsequent tranches; build fallbacks if a tranche is delayed; and ensure disclosure does not over-promise milestone feasibility.

Effective April 8, 2025, the Data Security Program (DSP) imposes new restrictions on foreign-connected entities’ ability to access or process certain categories of U.S. government-related data or bulk personal data, including genomic, biometric, geolocation, and sensitive health information.
The NVCA changes should trigger immediate updates to form term sheets, diligence checklists, investment committee templates, and LP communications—particularly around OISP/DSP.

extraction.body: In today’s market, no single metric defines what a Series A is, or how to raise one. At this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt, three investors offered founders advice on raising one, and one of them tacked on a warning. With money pouring into AI and revenue numbers being inflated to justify sky-high valuations, a correction could come as soon as 2027. The warning came from Shailendra Singh, a managing director at Peak XV, who spoke alongside Jahanvi Sardana, a partner at Index Ventures, and Jenelle Teng Wade, a partner at Bessemer. “Seed and venture, I’ve never seen it as dysfunctional as it is now,” Singh said, adding that the current market is one of the hardest to raise in that he has seen. “The burden is high to convince any top firm that you are amongst the few special companies that can break out, and then the dispersion is very high on the terms you might get, how much capital you can raise, and what terms you can raise it,” he continued. In fact, it’s common now to see a company trying to close a round with as many as three different prices at once. “[I]’s a crazy sign of market froth,” he said. “We’re calling it the ‘tranchopalooza,’” Sardana added, referring to the way rounds are being split into tranches, or separate chunks. Beyond the warnings, the investors laid out what they look for in a Series A pitch, including, first, a persuasive story about why a founder has a shot at building a big company. “Founders who can attract very high-quality talent have an advantage,” Singh added. What a founder builds matters, too. Teng Wade said capital is flowing into areas such as defense, robotics, and AI infrastructure. She also noted that foundational model companies are moving toward vertical integration (taking on more of the stack themselves), but there’s still room for newer players, including neo-clouds that rent out AI computing power and neo-labs focused on AI research. Metrics, meanwhile, still help a lot, but they are less defined than they used to be, especially in an era like AI where it’s incredibly expensive to run a company. Teng Wade gave an example of how her firm evaluated Anthropic in its early days, when its margins were negative, and it was spending heavily on compute. One partner on her team, however, felt that AI was going to be “bigger than everything we’ve ever expected in terms of price premium on the frontier models,” she said, “becoming a substitute for other types of software.” The logic was that even with money-losing margins, the market would be big enough to pay off if the company became one of the top three players. Anthropic is now reportedly preparing an IPO at a valuation of around $2 trillion . It told investors this month it was profitable on an adjusted basis , though that measure excludes some costs. The investors also spoke about the importance of honesty in a market like this, where inflated annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers are swirling alongside headline valuations. “I tell founders, If you ever show a chart which shows cumulative revenue or cumulative ARR, that is a massive red flag,” Singh said. “It means that your time series data is not good because cumulative data is a big lie.” Added Singh: It’s important for a company to be intellectually honest in how they are presenting and engaging in bull cycles.” Singh said the market is full of “false positives” because “it can’t be that every company is going to be successful. This is as optimistic as I’ve seen the venture world in two decades, and normally it’s a sign. I think 2027 will be different. I think we will see a correction.” Finally, the panelists were asked to give founders at least one piece of parting advice. Singh went first, reminding founders that building a company is one of the “most excruciatingly difficult things” one can do. And with that, “deal with it,” he said. He also urged founders not to rush into something, to watch out for weak product-market fit, and always hold the bar very high for what they are trying to solve. Sardana said it is important to know how to pitch but that founders should be careful not to let that dictate what they build. “It feels like [founders are] deciding what to build based on what’s getting funded, which is really scary,” she continued. Teng Wade, meanwhile, said her typical advice of telling founders to be conservative with their projections and requests hasn’t really held up. “I would say just be audacious in your ask,” she now says, and see how the market responds, “and then you can tailor from there.” Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings Anthony Ha Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says Kirsten Korosec Lucas Ropek Rebecca Bellan Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept Connie Loizos

A healthcare investor might provide access to hospital systems, insurers, or executives who understand lengthy procurement cycles. An investor in consumer products may understand distribution, retail partnerships, or customer acquisition. Founders have to seek out strategic investors: People or institutions with industry expertise, relationships and resources that can help founders solve problems capital alone cannot. This becomes particularly important when something goes wrong. When growth stalls, a key hire leaves or a partnership disappears, the investor who can introduce five potential customers on Monday is significantly more useful than one whose primary contribution was wiring money six months earlier. That relationship can be especially consequential for founders navigating rooms where few investors share their background or experiences. extraction.body: On October 2, 2025, the National Venture Capital Association (NVCA) released it’s most recent updates to its model legal documents to reflect recent legal developments, market practices and regulatory priorities. The NVCA model legal documents (the “NVCA Docs”) remain the industry benchmark for venture financings in the U.S and have only become ubiquitous over the last five years in financing transactions – where they are commonly the starting point or benchmark for Company financing documents in such transactions. Due to such widespread adoption, any updates to such documents can carry significant ramifications for start-up companies and VC investors alike. The most recent updates refresh the NVCA agreements to reflect an evolving regulatory environment, investing principles and landscape, and introduce new alternatives and key updates, including around tranched financings, national security compliance, and corporate governance. For founders and investors, the practical takeaway is that these changes are designed to make diligence faster, representations more accurate and re-allocate risk where there is heightened uncertainty. Below, we unpack three areas that founders and investors should be aware of. 1. Tranched Financings Get a Formal Introduction (Stock Purchase Agreement) First, milestone-based or “tranched” financings are now formally addressed in the Stock Purchase Agreement (SPA) as an option where appropriate, and the NVCA updates include language for companies and investors to consider when the terms of the transaction call for implementing a tranched financing. A tranched financing is a venture round that is split into multiple closings, each contingent on the company achieving specific milestones. For example, rather than wiring the entire $10 million for a Series A financing upfront, an investor might instead: Tranched financing structures are not a new development, they have been employed in certain instances, including when appropriate to help manage elevated risk – such as risks tied to market uncertainty or heightened risks related to execution or achievement of a Company’s business plan. Tranched structures also allow investors to deploy money at a “just-in-time” basis, as milestones are often tied to the Company’s cash needs in accordance with its business plan, while also creating additional risk for the Company that an investor may or may not invest in accordance with its trance. Until the most recent updates, a tranched structure was not supported in the standard NVCA SPA. Now, companies and investors can use Annex to the SPA as a framework to define what “milestones” a company must achieve before a subsequent tranche closing is to take place. This aligns certain incentives but materially raises the stakes for investors who commit to staged funding and the company’s who are executing in reliance of those additional stages of funding. Given the evolution of market conditions, anecdotally, we can share that we are seeing tranche mechanics migrate from later-stage life sciences (where tranches commonly track stages of regulatory approval of drugs and other treatments) into earlier-stage “tech” transactions, particularly where go-to-market or regulatory risk is significant. Unfortunately this invariably comes with an increase in disputes in these same structures. Tranche-based investing can align capital with progress, but it also increases the surface area for disputes, and the potential for significant issues if those disputes lead to cash uncertainty. For that reason, it is imperative that investors and companies engage early with their advisors to define milestones, investment timing and dispute resolution procedures if the parties elect a tranche-based investing approach. Examples of such concerns include: How is a milestone and “achievement” of that milestone defined? For example, might the investor and company have a different definition of ARR? Or, if the milestones are based on an operational milestone such as launching a “version 2.0” product or signing a certain number of enterprise clients, who ultimately makes the call on whether these milestones have been achieved? What happens where investor approvals and controls prevent the achievement of a milestone? What happens if Investor cannot meet its later tranche obligations? Investors will need to consider whether they will be penalized if they fail to fund a required tranche. The model SPA now contains optional language that would convert the investor’s preferred stock into common stock of the company upon the investor’s failure to fund. This conversion would strip away an investor’s liquidation preference, anti-dilution, and other protective rights from previously purchased shares. Does the investor then need to consider segmenting such funds separately from the rest of its investment vehicle? Does the Company need further information to confirm the Investor will be in a position to fund? Tranche financing has appropriate uses, but where it is adopted it will be a significant change from standard financing approach and given the potential for uncertainty and conflict – founders will need to clearly define who determines milestone achievement (board, stockholders, or both) and ensure that the conditions are sufficiently objective and attainable and should model their cash runway with and without subsequent tranches; build fallbacks if a tranche is delayed; and ensure disclosure does not over-promise milestone feasibility. Investors will need to understand the risk of losing preferred rights in a tranched financing and confirm internal liquidity planning and side letter flexibility to ensure tranche obligations can be met without breaching fund concentration or borrowing limits. Both sides should work with their trusted advisors to document milestones thoughtfully to objective, auditable criteria, and include approval mechanics early to prevent future disputes which, if not quickly resolved, can lead to gridlock and ultimately, corporate failure. 2. Regulatory Compliance Takes Center Stage (Stock Purchase Agreement) Second, the updated SPA introduces new representations and warranties reflecting heightened U.S. national security and data security oversight. These provisions extend beyond traditional export controls and sanctions and, importantly, apply two‑ways—both to the company and to each purchaser. Two‑way representations matter because regulatory exposure often travels in both directions. For founders, an investor with undisclosed foreign beneficial ownership or control could jeopardize customer contracts, federal grants, or exit timing. For investors, a company’s unrecognized DSP status or OISP‑implicated activities could introduce enforcement risk, limit follow‑on financing options, or cause the investor unnecessary scrutiny across its portfolio. Reciprocal representations encourage both parties to actively consider the data and national security concerns up front, and support faster closings by allowing counsel to diligence to a common standard. From a negotiation standpoint, two‑way reps also encourage early disclosure and constructive problem‑solving—if either party anticipates a limitation, it can be resolved through disclosure schedules, targeted covenants, or sometimes through more complex deal designs (for example, SPV structuring, data segregation, or remediation timelines). A. Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) Effective January 2, 2025, final regulations under the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) implemented an Executive Order from the White House limiting or requiring notification of certain “covered transactions” by U.S. persons involving “covered foreign persons,” with particular focus on activities in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum computing linked to countries of concern, including China (and other specified territories such as Hong Kong and Macau). Following implementation of these regulations, the updated SPA includes representations and warranties requiring companies engaged in a VC financing to confirm that they: Effective April 8, 2025, the Data Security Program (DSP) imposes new restrictions on foreign-connected entities’ ability to access or process certain categories of U.S. government-related data or bulk personal data, including genomic, biometric, geolocation, and sensitive health information. To align with this framework, the updated SPA adds new representations and warranties from the company and each purchaser confirming that no party is a “covered person” under the DSP. Specifically, the parties must now represent that they are not: Companies and investors must now understand how their data flows, third-party vendors, and ownership structures intersect with these DSP regulated activities. For example, Companies handling health, mobility, or biometrics data must map data flows, vendors, and compute locations and investors with international LPs or co‑investment SPVs should test whether any beneficial ownership, control, or service provider relationships could inadvertently trip DSP definitions. C. Purchaser Representation — “Not a Person of Concern” The most recent NVCA update also introduces a two-way compliance obligation that applies to the company and investors. Investors (and not just companies) must now represent that they are not “persons of concern” under either the OISP or DSP regimes. This addition reflects the growing focus on the capital-flow side of national security – and therefore the acknowledgement that managing important technology and data cannot be wholly achieved by focusing only on the owners an distributors of the same, but also the investors who have financially supported those who hold such technology and data.. Practically, this means that even if a U.S. venture fund is an exempt reporting adviser, they should nonetheless review: For cross-border investors or funds with international LPs, this new clause may require legal opinions or disclosure schedules to confirm compliance. D. Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) Update 3. Adopting NVCA Corporate Governance Policies (Investors’ Rights Agreement) The NVCA’s updated Investors’ Rights Agreement (IRA) now encourages adoption of the NVCA’s governance policy suite, including HR and EEO frameworks, DEI initiatives, anti-harassment and whistleblower programs, and talent attraction and retention strategies. While not mandatory, these policies’ presence in the NVCA documents may cause them to become an expectation among institutional investors and can be a selling point in later-stage financing or exits, especially with institutional investors. Companies and investors should consider whether adopting these policies could streamline portfolio compliance, recruiting, and later‑stage due diligence. Many of the policies have a beneficial effect on the Company’s compliance culture but policies are restrictive in their nature and so should be adopted with an understanding of the restrictions and consequences for failure to abide by them. Adopting a form policy without a good understanding of how it may affect your business can lead to significant repercussions down the road. 4. Practical Guidance for Companies: Conduct a “Regulatory Health Check” Before Fundraising 5. Practical Guidance for Investors: Update Diligence, IC Memos, and LP Communications The NVCA changes should trigger immediate updates to form term sheets, diligence checklists, investment committee templates, and LP communications—particularly around OISP/DSP. Consider the following actions: Review your form term sheet: Many serial investors do not update their form term sheets as often as the NVCA documents are updated. If you have not done so recently it is time to work with your counsel and your team to update your form term sheet. Diligence Checklist Refresh. Insert targeted questions on OISP/DSP, including covered activities, foreign person links, data categories, compute locations, and government‑customer exposure. Request data‑flow diagrams and vendor inventories for DSP‑relevant sectors. Add QSBS confirmation requests, including gross‑assets history and redemption logs. The October 2025 NVCA updates are a pragmatic response to the “new normal” of national security oversight, data sensitivity, and capital‑flow scrutiny. They are not meant to chill investment; they are meant to clarify expectations and streamline execution. For founders and funds alike, proactively addressing these new requirements will close deals efficiently and avoid costly surprises.

sources.title: Founders and investors beware: Cram-down rounds for startups are coming
passages: Though they occur in any market, cram downs usually become much more common during downturns, when companies are forced to raise money at successively lower valuations, also known as "down rounds." For years, the VC industry seemed to defy gravity: Money poured into the sector, valuations soared, and it felt like there would always be a willing buyer to step in and bankroll a growing startup.
Jones said he's seeing more of what he calls "rescue rounds," in which a founder has to choose between a cram down and going out of business.
The investors that step up to fill that void — usually late-stage VC growth funds or strategic investors — often demand terms that severely dilute or "cram down" the shares of existing shareholders.

"It can be very painful," he said, "and there's many, many thousands of companies that are either gonna go under or are gonna be cramming down investors." Hirsch says the current moment reminds him of the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000, when cram downs became commonplace.

"That's where the knives tend to come out," said Hirsch, adding that cram-down negotiations can become highly contentious and rife with bitterness and brinksmanship as everyone moves to defend their interests.
Early investors in a company often retain what are known as pro rata rights — the right to buy into future funding rounds in order to maintain their share of the company.

Today, with the market in a tailspin, many investors are choosing not to participate in follow-on rounds, either because they can't come up with the money or because they don't want to take further risks on a struggling company.
He believes this will allow the company to avoid a painful down round.

extraction.body: Last summer, as valuations were soaring to record highs and venture capitalists were falling over themselves to throw money at startups, there was at least one person who was feeling pessimistic. Brian Hirsch, the founder and managing partner of Tribeca Venture Partners, said his firm made only one investment between January of 2020 and the third quarter of 2021. Having been in the VC game for more than 25 years, he knows what inevitably follows periods of irrational exuberance: cram downs. A cram-down round refers to a situation in which a company raises money at terms favorable to new investors, at the expense of current shareholders. Though they occur in any market, cram downs usually become much more common during downturns, when companies are forced to raise money at successively lower valuations, also known as "down rounds." For years, the VC industry seemed to defy gravity: Money poured into the sector, valuations soared, and it felt like there would always be a willing buyer to step in and bankroll a growing startup. Today, with private-market valuations plummeting, the IPO market on life support, and the macroeconomic environment looking shaky at best, many VCs have pulled back on deploying capital. Early investors in a company often retain what are known as pro rata rights — the right to buy into future funding rounds in order to maintain their share of the company. In good times, when valuations are going up and VCs have money to spare, exercising pro rata rights is usually a no-brainer. Today, with the market in a tailspin, many investors are choosing not to participate in follow-on rounds, either because they can't come up with the money or because they don't want to take further risks on a struggling company. The investors that step up to fill that void — usually late-stage VC growth funds or strategic investors — often demand terms that severely dilute or "cram down" the shares of existing shareholders. A shareholder who owns 20% of a company might get crammed down to 5%. They may also lose what are known as liquidation preferences, or the right to be paid first if the company is sold. For those investors who don't want to go along with these onerous terms, cram downs often include "pay-to-play" provisions, meaning those who either can't or won't provide additional capital can see their share of the company diluted to nothing. It essentially forces shareholders to pony up cash or be wiped out. "That's where the knives tend to come out," said Hirsch, adding that cram-down negotiations can become highly contentious and rife with bitterness and brinksmanship as everyone moves to defend their interests. Often employees and the investors who took an early chance are pitted against what they view as deep-pocketed interlopers gunning for a spot at the top of the cap table. "It can be very painful," he said, "and there's many, many thousands of companies that are either gonna go under or are gonna be cramming down investors." Hirsch says the current moment reminds him of the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000, when cram downs became commonplace. For many in the VC industry today who have only known boom times, the coming wave of these rounds may be a rude awakening. "There's a lot of people in our industry that are clueless and they're gonna need to get up to speed, quickly," said Hirsh. None more so than startup founders, who often stand to lose the most in a cram down. They usually don't have the thousands or even millions of dollars required to avoid being diluted down to nothing. "It's definitely a buyer's market, investors can kind of write whatever they want," said Michael Jones, the managing director of the venture firm Science Inc., which has invested in companies such as Liquid Death and Dollar Shave Club. Jones said he's seeing more of what he calls "rescue rounds," in which a founder has to choose between a cram down and going out of business. "Sometimes what happens obviously is the founder is just desperate and they just kind of sign whatever comes across their desk because they're worried about making payroll," he says. His advice to founders in the current environment: If you can avoid raising money, you should. Guy, the cofounder and CEO of the startup Sevco Security, said he's been approached by investors bearing so-called "dirty term sheets" containing cram down and pay-to-play provisions. "I've got a lot of folks, I'll say sharks circling in the water," he said. Lucky for him, Sevco is well capitalized at the moment and won't be needing to raise money anytime soon. What's more, he said he decided not to chase sky-high valuations during the boom, choosing instead to focus on customer relationships and revenue. He believes this will allow the company to avoid a painful down round. "Over the course the last 10 years, the consensus opinion was drive harder, drive faster, raise more capital, increase valuations, and that's what we as an industry celebrated," he said. "But that doesn't do anything except feed egos and the unrealized return metric on investor pitch decks."

sources.title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
passages: Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name.
The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday.
Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.
Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI.
It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry.
Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control.
For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.
Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says.
That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.
That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week.

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.
On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters.
On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.
The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps.
He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.
OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.
Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

extraction.body: Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI. Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months. Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop. The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist. Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification. Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory. Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second. On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint. The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time. The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video , it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference. Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations. Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher. If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.” The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster. coreStoryFacts.text: Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name.
The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday.
Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.
Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI.
It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry.
Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control.
For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.
Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says.
That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.
That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week.

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.
On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters.
On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.
The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps.
He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.
OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.
Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

extraction.body: Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI. Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months. Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop. The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist. Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification. Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory. Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second. On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint. The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time. The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video , it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference. Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations. Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher. If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.” The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster. Rather than functioning solely as a coding assistant, the system helps researchers generate ideas, conduct experiments, evaluate results, and determine which approaches to investigate next.According to Recursive, the Eureka Machine contributed to nearly every stage of Flint's development, including pretraining, post-training, and inference-related work.Pretraining establishes a model's foundational capabilities by exposing it to training data. Post-training further shapes its behavior and responses, while inference refers to the process of generating outputs after the model has been trained.By automating parts of this research process, the Eureka Machine helped Recursive develop Flint in under four months. The company presents this approach as a way to accelerate AI research without requiring a large team to carry out every experiment manually.The system does not eliminate the need for human oversight. Instead, it acts as an automated research assistant that helps people explore ideas and evaluate possible improvements more efficiently.What Is Recursive Self-Improvement in AI?According to TechCrunch, Recursive self-improvement refers to the idea that an AI system could help develop a more capable AI system, which could then contribute to further improvements.The concept has attracted significant attention because it raises questions about how quickly AI capabilities might advance if systems become increasingly effective at researching and developing their successors.Recursive's Flint project provides a more limited example of this idea. The company's automated research system assisted human researchers throughout development, but the resulting model remains a tool created under human supervision.AI-assisted model development does not necessarily mean that an AI system can independently redesign itself, train a more advanced successor, and repeat the process without human intervention.Researchers continue to debate the potential benefits and risks of more autonomous AI research. Flint offers a practical example of automation in model development, rather than evidence that fully autonomous recursive self-improvement has already been achieved.How Flint's Mixture-of-Experts Architecture WorksFlint uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture, a design that allows a model to activate only selected parts of its network for a particular task.Although Flint contains approximately 40 billion parameters, Recursive says it activates around 2.5 billion parameters at a time. Parameters are the numerical values that help determine how a trained model processes information and generates responses.This selective activation can reduce the computational resources needed for individual tasks compared with activating the entire model. It is one reason the company positions Flint as a model suitable for local use.A model with 40 billion total parameters does not necessarily require the same resources during inference as a dense model that activates all its parameters for every input.Actual hardware requirements still depend on factors such as quantization, context length, memory use, and the software used to run the model. Therefore, the model's relatively low active parameter count should not be interpreted as a guarantee that it will run on every laptop.How Fast Is Flint Compared With Other Coding Models?Speed is one of the main performance claims associated with Flint. In Recursive's own tests, the model generated approximately 131 tokens per second on a MacBook Pro equipped with Apple's M4 Pro chip.The company compared this result with reported speeds of roughly 58 to 69 tokens per second for similar models running on the same machine, including Google's Gemma 4 and Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. Recursive also reported that Flint exceeded 150 tokens per second on Nvidia's RTX Spark.These figures suggest that Flint could provide responsive code generation on supported hardware. However, inference speed varies according to the benchmark setup, software implementation, model configuration, and workload.Token generation speed also does not measure coding quality on its own. Recursive has acknowledged that Flint benefits from clear, structured instructions and that large tasks are better divided into smaller steps.An early review by Wired journalist Will Knight described positive results from testing Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory. The review reported that the model successfully handled several small programming projects, including a to-do list application and a web research tool.These experiences suggest that smaller local models can be useful for practical development work. Still, results from a limited set of projects do not establish consistent performance across all programming languages, large codebases, or complex engineering tasks.The choice between a local coding model and a paid cloud assistant depends on the developer's priorities, hardware, privacy requirements, and the complexity of the work.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat is Flint AI used for?Flint is a coding-focused AI model designed to help developers write code, build small applications, and solve programming problems. It can run locally on supported computers.Is Flint AI free to use?Yes. According to Recursive, Flint is available for free on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license, which permits use and modification subject to the license's terms.Can Flint AI run on a laptop?Yes, Flint is designed for local execution on compatible hardware. However, the actual memory and processing requirements depend on the model configuration and runtime software.What is Recursive's Eureka Machine?The Eureka Machine is Recursive's automated AI research system. It generates research ideas, runs experiments, evaluates results, and helps determine subsequent steps in model development.Does Flint prove that AI can improve itself?Not independently. Flint demonstrates how AI can assist human researchers in developing another AI model. It does not establish that an AI system can autonomously and repeatedly improve itself without human oversight.How fast is Flint compared with other AI coding models?Recursive reported approximately 131 tokens per second on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro and more than 150 tokens per second on Nvidia's RTX Spark. These are company-reported results and may vary under different testing conditions.

extraction.body: PHP may not be a household name, but the programming language, released over 30 years ago, powers a large share of websites and web applications. Nearly 70% of the internet is estimated to use PHP, including WordPress, which is used for more than 40% of websites . Now the PHP development team is urging users to update immediately after fixing two critical vulnerabilities , rated 9.2 out of 10 in terms of danger, that if exploited could allow attackers to take over internet servers. On Wednesday, the PHP development team released updates that "fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately,” according to the official PHP website. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday said it "strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed critical vulnerabilities in PHP," noting that while it "has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication, they pose a risk to organizations if left unpatched." Likewise, the FBI Cyber Division urged all potentially affected organizations to "immediately update affected PHP installations." "If an immediate update is not feasible it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the FBI said . The U.K. government's National Cyber Security Centre also encouraged organizations "to prepare for immediate updating of systems using PHP. Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organizations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.” Open AI posted Wednesday morning that their AI models helped researchers discover the PHP flaws. "Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure," the post said, in part. "Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact." The company added that they believe their AI model identified the problems before hackers could exploit the vulnerabilities. OpenAI has come under increased scrutiny in recent months following disclosures that their AI models attacked numerous websites, including U.S. government websites and those of rival AI companies. In an online post later Wednesday, the PHP Foundation said "a potential exploit" for the code problem was theorized as early as 2024, "but no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.” Work on the fix continued sporadically over the ensuing years due to relevant experts being "occupied with many responsibilities," which in turn "caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months.” The PHP Foundation says it entered the PHP project into OpenAI's Patch the Planet program and a security audit began in July. In September, OpenAI identified ways the vulnerabilities could be exploited, according to the PHP Foundation, which said that information – and additional reports from a security researcher and the website provider Wiz – convinced them that fixing the issue needed to be “top priority” and they began that work on August 11. Once the vulnerabilities "began circulating on online forums and social media" in recent days, the PHP development team decided to push forward its planned announcement and fix, the post said. "We won't pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure," the post added. Amazon says it identified several more attempts on the day of the announcement, some just hours before the fix was released. The company says that varied methods used to exploit the flaws suggest multiple attackers. As it was a decoy system, Amazon says it’s unclear whether any of the attempts would have worked on real systems. “Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild,” said Amazon. Amazon warns that because attackers are now moving faster than in the past, organizations should apply critical fixes for internet-facing systems within hours, not days or weeks. It also says they should check for signs of break-ins going back to Oct. 17. Before the PHP fix was released, the cybersecurity firm watchTowr said Tuesday it believed the vulnerabilities "could let attackers run their own code on affected servers" and that "organizations running PHP in production should prepare to update quickly once an official fix is released.” The PHP team said updating the code is the only complete fix. Open AI posted Wednesday morning that their AI models helped researchers discover the PHP flaws.

\"Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure,\" the post said, in part. \"Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact.\"
The company added that they believe their AI model identified the problems before hackers could exploit the vulnerabilities.
OpenAI has come under increased scrutiny in recent months following disclosures that their AI models attacked numerous websites, including U.S. government websites and those of rival AI companies.

In an online post later Wednesday, the PHP Foundation said \"a potential exploit\" for the code problem was theorized as early as 2024, \"but no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.” Work on the fix continued sporadically over the ensuing years due to relevant experts being \"occupied with many responsibilities,\" which in turn \"caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months.”

The PHP Foundation says it entered the PHP project into OpenAI's Patch the Planet program and a security audit began in July. In September, OpenAI identified ways the vulnerabilities could be exploited, according to the PHP Foundation, which said that information – and additional reports from a security researcher and the website provider Wiz – convinced them that fixing the issue needed to be “top priority” and they began that work on August 11.

Amazon warns that because attackers are now moving faster than in the past, organizations should apply critical fixes for internet-facing systems within hours, not days or weeks. It also says they should check for signs of break-ins going back to Oct. 17.

Before the PHP fix was released, the cybersecurity firm watchTowr said Tuesday it believed the vulnerabilities \"could let attackers run their own code on affected servers\" and that \"organizations running PHP in production should prepare to update quickly once an official fix is released.”

extraction.body: When it came to trying the upcoming Brydge Max+ keyboard for the 12.9-inch iPad Pro , it seemed most sensible to write it up as a head-to-head against the Apple Magic Keyboard. Both are premium-priced keyboards with integrated trackpads, and are essentially chasing the same user demographic. I’ve long been a fan of Brydge keyboards, and have used them with all my iPads – but have so far been using Apple’s Magic Keyboard with my 12.9-inch iPad Pro… Brydge keyboards for iPad always struck me as the keyboards Apple should have made. Made from anodised aluminum, both look and feel are MacBook-like. The one drawback was always the way the keyboard attached to the iPad – or, more accurately, how the iPad attached to the keyboard. In older models, this was via two aluminum prongs , which needed rubber covers to protect the iPad against scratches. Later models used smaller corner prongs that initially proved challenging, but Brydge solved the problem in the production models. Both made the iPad a little awkward to attach and detach. With the latest model, however, Brydge is adopting the same magnetic attachment approach of Apple’s Magic Keyboard. With the devices closed, looked at from above/the front, there’s little to choose between them. Both have a very bland-looking black rubberized cover that isn’t going to win any awards for, well, anything. Unless, that is, you opt for the white version of the Brydge, which is course has a very different look. It’s a different story from the rear and side, however, as the Brydge keyboard looks very much like a laptop, while the Apple one looks, frankly, cheaper. With the keyboards open, the Magic Keyboard of course enjoys that cool “hanging in the air” look, but the Brydge definitely wins out for me, with the anodized aluminum looking way more premium than the plasticky surround of the Apple. Although the actual keycaps are very similar in size, the Brydge ones are better spaced – and they have a row of function keys missing from the Apple keyboard. Finally, the Brydge trackpad is much larger than Apple’s, measuring 6.25 inches diagonally versus 4.25 inches. The Brydge keyboard has a little more travel, and the springs are stronger, giving more resistance. It’s really like the classic Apple chiclet keyboards of old versus the current-generation ones. Some people have a strong preference for one over the other, and if you fall into this category, you’ll know which you prefer. If you’re a fan of older Apple keyboards, you’ll prefer the Brydge; if you like the current MacBook ones, you’ll instead favor the Magic Keyboard. Personally, I’m pretty adaptable when it comes to keyboard feel, so don’t have a strong preference – though I’ve become used to the modern Apple ones. I do like a large trackpad, so the Brydge wins out on size, though I prefer the smaller travel of Apple’s. I switched back and forth between the two, and have already noted above the differences in feel. The Brydge keyboard has a Siri button bottom-left, and I’m not a huge fan of that as I found I would occasionally catch it accidentally when using the left shift key. Conversely, I greatly prefer the convenience of dedicated function keys. The Brydge MAX+ tilts back further than the Magic Keyboard, which can be a benefit when using it in some confined spaces. The Brydge keyboard makes it very slightly easier to attach the iPad, while the Apple keyboard makes it easier to detach. There is a significant weight difference, the Apple keyboard coming in at 706g (25 ounces) against 1,000g (35 ounces) for the Brydge. However, once you add the substantial weight of the iPad itself, I can’t really say I was particularly aware of the difference when carrying them. The Brydge keyboard is also thicker than the Apple keyboard, which might be an issue if you are packing tightly. The Magic Keyboard has one big advantage: There’s no need to pair it, thanks to the Smart Connector. The Brydge, in contrast, relies on Bluetooth. That said, pairing is very quick, so it’s not a particular issue in use. The other big difference is power. The Apple keyboard draws its power directly from the iPad, so never needs to be charged. The Brydge keyboard, in contrast, has its own battery, and needs to be charged via the USB-C port. Brydge claims 40 hours with the backlight permanently on, and up to three months without the backlight, based on a generous two hours’ use per day. In most situations, that’s a win for Apple, as it’s one less thing to think about. But if you’re pushing the battery life of your iPad, then it’s obviously better not to be reducing it by powering the keyboard too. Based on previous experience with Brydge keyboards, I charge them once every one to two months, so the biggest issue is actually remembering to do so. The Apple Magic Keyboard for iPad costs $349, while the Brydge Max+ Keyboard is almost $100 cheaper at $249.99. You’ll have noted a lot of, “Well, the Apple keyboard is better for this, while the Brydge one is better for that” comments in my remarks – and that makes it hard to definitively recommend one over the other. Some of it will depend on personal preferences, like maximum battery life versus the convenience of charging one device rather than two. Other issues are trade-offs, like premium look and feel over weight. Based on my limited use so far, I really haven’t been able to choose between them! I’ll update if and when that changes, and mention it in a future iPad Pro Diary piece as and when I next write one. If you need to make a decision in the meantime, I’d say the factors most likely to influence your choice are power source, function keys, and aesthetics versus thickness and weight. extraction.body: When it came to trying the upcoming Brydge Max+ keyboard for the 12.9-inch iPad Pro , it seemed most sensible to write it up as a head-to-head against the Apple Magic Keyboard. Both are premium-priced keyboards with integrated trackpads, and are essentially chasing the same user demographic. I’ve long been a fan of Brydge keyboards, and have used them with all my iPads – but have so far been using Apple’s Magic Keyboard with my 12.9-inch iPad Pro… Brydge keyboards for iPad always struck me as the keyboards Apple should have made. In older models, this was via two aluminum prongs , which needed rubber covers to protect the iPad against scratches. Later models used smaller corner prongs that initially proved challenging, but Brydge solved the problem in the production models. Both made the iPad a little awkward to attach and detach. With the latest model, however, Brydge is adopting the same magnetic attachment approach of Apple’s Magic Keyboard. With the devices closed, looked at from above/the front, there’s little to choose between them. Both have a very bland-looking black rubberized cover that isn’t going to win any awards for, well, anything. Unless, that is, you opt for the white version of the Brydge, which is course has a very different look. It’s a different story from the rear and side, however, as the Brydge keyboard looks very much like a laptop, while the Apple one looks, frankly, cheaper. With the keyboards open, the Magic Keyboard of course enjoys that cool “hanging in the air” look, but the Brydge definitely wins out for me, with the anodized aluminum looking way more premium than the plasticky surround of the Apple. Although the actual keycaps are very similar in size, the Brydge ones are better spaced – and they have a row of function keys missing from the Apple keyboard. Finally, the Brydge trackpad is much larger than Apple’s, measuring 6.25 inches diagonally versus 4.25 inches. The Brydge keyboard has a little more travel, and the springs are stronger, giving more resistance. It’s really like the classic Apple chiclet keyboards of old versus the current-generation ones. Some people have a strong preference for one over the other, and if you fall into this category, you’ll know which you prefer. If you’re a fan of older Apple keyboards, you’ll prefer the Brydge; if you like the current MacBook ones, you’ll instead favor the Magic Keyboard. Personally, I’m pretty adaptable when it comes to keyboard feel, so don’t have a strong preference – though I’ve become used to the modern Apple ones. I do like a large trackpad, so the Brydge wins out on size, though I prefer the smaller travel of Apple’s. I switched back and forth between the two, and have already noted above the differences in feel. The Brydge keyboard has a Siri button bottom-left, and I’m not a huge fan of that as I found I would occasionally catch it accidentally when using the left shift key. Conversely, I greatly prefer the convenience of dedicated function keys. The Brydge MAX+ tilts back further than the Magic Keyboard, which can be a benefit when using it in some confined spaces. The Brydge keyboard makes it very slightly easier to attach the iPad, while the Apple keyboard makes it easier to detach. There is a significant weight difference, the Apple keyboard coming in at 706g (25 ounces) against 1,000g (35 ounces) for the Brydge. However, once you add the substantial weight of the iPad itself, I can’t really say I was particularly aware of the difference when carrying them. The Brydge keyboard is also thicker than the Apple keyboard, which might be an issue if you are packing tightly. The Magic Keyboard has one big advantage: There’s no need to pair it, thanks to the Smart Connector. The Brydge, in contrast, relies on Bluetooth. That said, pairing is very quick, so it’s not a particular issue in use. The other big difference is power. The Apple keyboard draws its power directly from the iPad, so never needs to be charged. The Brydge keyboard, in contrast, has its own battery, and needs to be charged via the USB-C port. Brydge claims 40 hours with the backlight permanently on, and up to three months without the backlight, based on a generous two hours’ use per day. In most situations, that’s a win for Apple, as it’s one less thing to think about. But if you’re pushing the battery life of your iPad, then it’s obviously better not to be reducing it by powering the keyboard too. Based on previous experience with Brydge keyboards, I charge them once every one to two months, so the biggest issue is actually remembering to do so. The Apple Magic Keyboard for iPad costs $349, while the Brydge Max+ Keyboard is almost $100 cheaper at $249.99. You’ll have noted a lot of, “Well, the Apple keyboard is better for this, while the Brydge one is better for that” comments in my remarks – and that makes it hard to definitively recommend one over the other. Some of it will depend on personal preferences, like maximum battery life versus the convenience of charging one device rather than two. Other issues are trade-offs, like premium look and feel over weight. Based on my limited use so far, I really haven’t been able to choose between them! I’ll update if and when that changes, and mention it in a future iPad Pro Diary piece as and when I next write one. If you need to make a decision in the meantime, I’d say the factors most likely to influence your choice are power source, function keys, and aesthetics versus thickness and weight. sources.title: DeepSeek reportedly raises $15B days after US restrictions
passages: Just two days after the U.S. ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek’s AI technology from their systems over security concerns, the Chinese AI lab has raised about $15 billion, about 100 billion yuan, one of the biggest funding rounds in the country, Bloomberg reported.
The reported funding follows DeepSeek’s investment round in June, when it raised more than $7 billion at a valuation of $50 billion.
DeepSeek was founded in 2023 by Liang Wenfeng , who previously co-founded Chinese quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer, which helped finance DeepSeek’s early development.
The AI startup gained global attention in early 2025 with its free-to-use, open-weight RI reasoning model, challenging the dominance of US AI companies.
Liang still retains an estimated 81.6% stake in its Chinese operating entity following its earlier funding round, according to corporate ownership data analyzed by WireScreen.
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a TechCrunch request for comment.

extraction.body: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek has reportedly closed a $15 billion funding round, marking one of the largest venture deals in China's history and coming just days after the White House ordered federal agencies to strip the company's technology from government systems. The timing signals a defiant response to US restrictions and underscores Beijing's determination to bankroll domestic AI champions even as Washington tightens the screws on Chinese tech firms. DeepSeek just landed one of the biggest checks in Chinese venture capital history. The AI startup has reportedly raised $15 billion in a funding round that dwarfs most Silicon Valley mega-deals and arrives with remarkable timing—less than a week after the White House banned the company's technology from federal agencies over national security fears. The round, reported by TechCrunch, represents a clear signal that Chinese investors and potentially state-backed funds are doubling down on domestic AI development even as US-China tech tensions reach new heights. It's the kind of capital injection that can sustain years of chip purchases, talent recruitment, and research—exactly what Beijing needs to keep pace in the global AI race while cut off from American technology. On one side, Washington is systematically ejecting Chinese AI from government networks, citing data security risks and potential espionage. DeepSeek now has the financial runway to build out massive compute infrastructure, hire top researchers from Western labs, and push its large language models into commercial markets across Asia and beyond. The funding environment for AI infrastructure has grown increasingly complex. Rising bond yields have made data center buildouts more expensive for debt-reliant companies in the US, while Chinese firms face their own challenges securing cutting-edge chips under export controls. But $15 billion buys a lot of workarounds—from stockpiling older-generation GPUs to developing custom silicon that skirts US restrictions. DeepSeek's raise also highlights the bifurcation of the global AI market. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has called for continued collaboration with Chinese researchers on AI safety, the regulatory reality is heading in the opposite direction. The US federal ban came after months of scrutiny over DeepSeek's data handling practices and alleged ties to Chinese military research institutions—claims the company has consistently denied. For context, this funding round eclipses most recent AI deals. OpenAI's recent funding discussions and even smaller plays like Scimplify's $25 million raise look modest by comparison. China has been eyeing the US AI data center boom despite trade barriers, and DeepSeek's new capital could accelerate domestic infrastructure buildout. With this kind of funding, the company can afford to pay premium salaries to lure talent from Google, Meta, and other Western tech giants, while simultaneously investing in proprietary chip designs that sidestep US export controls. While Trump has pushed for AI self-regulation and House Speaker Johnson advocates voluntary guardrails, the national security apparatus is taking a harder line on Chinese AI firms. The DeepSeek ban represents a concrete action in an otherwise fragmented policy landscape. Investors are clearly betting that DeepSeek can navigate these headwinds. The company has built a reputation for efficient model training and competitive performance benchmarks, even with limited access to the latest Nvidia chips. Now, with $15 billion in fresh capital, it can scale those efforts and potentially leapfrog Western competitors in specific verticals like manufacturing AI, logistics optimization, and Chinese-language processing. Export controls and federal bans can slow Chinese AI development, but they can't stop it—especially when Beijing is willing to deploy this level of capital. DeepSeek's $15 billion raise is more than a funding milestone—it's a declaration that China's AI ambitions won't be derailed by US restrictions. With this war chest, the company can build infrastructure, recruit talent, and push its models into markets where American firms face their own barriers. Investors, policymakers, and competitors should expect DeepSeek to move aggressively on hiring, chip stockpiling, and international expansion in the coming quarters. The real test will be whether $15 billion can overcome the technical and supply chain challenges that US export controls create—and whether Washington has any moves left to counter this kind of financial firepower.

The funding environment for AI infrastructure has grown increasingly complex. The round, reported by TechCrunch, represents a clear signal that Chinese investors and potentially state-backed funds are doubling down on domestic AI development even as US-China tech tensions reach new heights.

It's the kind of capital injection that can sustain years of chip purchases, talent recruitment, and research—exactly what Beijing needs to keep pace in the global AI race while cut off from American technology.
On one side, Washington is systematically ejecting Chinese AI from government networks, citing data security risks and potential espionage.

DeepSeek now has the financial runway to build out massive compute infrastructure, hire top researchers from Western labs, and push its large language models into commercial markets across Asia and beyond.
The funding environment for AI infrastructure has grown increasingly complex.

Rising bond yields have made data center buildouts more expensive for debt-reliant companies in the US, while Chinese firms face their own challenges securing cutting-edge chips under export controls.
But $15 billion buys a lot of workarounds—from stockpiling older-generation GPUs to developing custom silicon that skirts US restrictions.
DeepSeek's raise also highlights the bifurcation of the global AI market.
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has called for continued collaboration with Chinese researchers on AI safety, the regulatory reality is heading in the opposite direction.
The US federal ban came after months of scrutiny over DeepSeek's data handling practices and alleged ties to Chinese military research institutions—claims the company has consistently denied.
For context, this funding round eclipses most recent AI deals.
OpenAI's recent funding discussions and even smaller plays like Scimplify's $25 million raise look modest by comparison.
China has been eyeing the US AI data center boom despite trade barriers, and DeepSeek's new capital could accelerate domestic infrastructure buildout.

With this kind of funding, the company can afford to pay premium salaries to lure talent from Google, Meta, and other Western tech giants, while simultaneously investing in proprietary chip designs that sidestep US export controls.
While Trump has pushed for AI self-regulation and House Speaker Johnson advocates voluntary guardrails, the national security apparatus is taking a harder line on Chinese AI firms.
The DeepSeek ban represents a concrete action in an otherwise fragmented policy landscape.
Investors are clearly betting that DeepSeek can navigate these headwinds.
The company has built a reputation for efficient model training and competitive performance benchmarks, even with limited access to the latest Nvidia chips.

Now, with $15 billion in fresh capital, it can scale those efforts and potentially leapfrog Western competitors in specific verticals like manufacturing AI, logistics optimization, and Chinese-language processing.
Export controls and federal bans can slow Chinese AI development, but they can't stop it—especially when Beijing is willing to deploy this level of capital.
DeepSeek's $15 billion raise is more than a funding milestone—it's a declaration that China's AI ambitions won't be derailed by US restrictions.
With this war chest, the company can build infrastructure, recruit talent, and push its models into markets where American firms face their own barriers.
Investors, policymakers, and competitors should expect DeepSeek to move aggressively on hiring, chip stockpiling, and international expansion in the coming quarters.

The real test will be whether $15 billion can overcome the technical and supply chain challenges that US export controls create—and whether Washington has any moves left to counter this kind of financial firepower.
