sources.title: South Korea Crypto Bill 2026: Digital Asset Basic Act - shattered.io
passages: South Korea’s long-awaited Digital Asset Basic Act is entering its final stretch.

On October 22, 2026, Lee Eog-weon, chairman of the Financial Services Commission (FSC) , told lawmakers that government consultations on the bill were nearing completion and that officials would push to introduce the legislation as quickly as possible.

The bill is still a proposal, not a signed law, but its shape is now public enough to map out what it would change for crypto exchanges, stablecoin issuers, and the software teams that build on top of both.

South Korea has one of the most active retail crypto markets in Asia, and its current rules, built around 2021-era reporting requirements for virtual-asset service providers, were never designed for a market with regulated won-stablecoins, bank-led consortia, and AI-driven trading tools.

According to a report from Bitcoin Foundation , the bill would cover digital-asset issuance, distribution, disclosure, exchange licensing, and stablecoin issuance in a single framework, replacing the patchwork of guidance exchanges have operated under for years.
South Korea did not start regulating crypto in 2026.
A second wave followed with the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, which focused on custody segregation and market-abuse rules for listed exchanges.

Teams working on exchange APIs, KYC pipelines, and on-chain settlement tooling in South Korea should expect new disclosure fields, stricter identity-verification hooks, and, if the stablecoin provisions pass as described, a defined reserve-attestation interface that bank-majority issuers will need to expose to regulators and, likely, to the public.

That is a familiar pattern for engineers who have already built compliance tooling against MiCA’s reserve-reporting requirements in Europe or the reserve-disclosure rules under the US federal stablecoin framework.

It is the same category of work covered in shattered.io’s broader software and developer-tooling coverage , and it overlaps heavily with the account-security hardening described in a 12-step guide to crypto exchange account security .
It is a comprehensive rewrite of how South Korea classifies and licenses anything built on blockchain rails.
The new bill goes further by trying to define, in law, what counts as a digital asset and which activities around it require formal authorization.

Reports indicate lawmakers and officials are also debating a virtual-asset tax scheduled to take effect in January 2027, with concerns raised about unclear standards and whether exchanges have built the reporting infrastructure in time.
He also framed the FSC’s position as a middle path between unchecked expansion and overcaution, telling lawmakers:

MiCA does not require banks to hold a majority stake in an e-money token issuer, and the US framework likewise allows non-bank entities to issue payment stablecoins under its own chartering and reserve rules.
For engineering teams at Korean exchanges, that distinction is not academic.
A reporting-only regime lets a platform ship new listing and custody features first and clean up compliance paperwork later.
A licensing regime, by contrast, forces legal review into the release cycle for anything touching asset issuance or disclosure.
South Korea is not writing stablecoin and exchange rules in a vacuum.
The European Union has run its Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, known as MiCA, since 2024, setting licensing and reserve standards across the bloc.
Three disputes remain unresolved, and any one of them could push introduction past whatever timeline the FSC is hoping for.
First, the stablecoin-issuer structure: whether banks get majority control, a lower minority stake, or a licensing path open to qualified non-bank firms.
Second, exchange shareholder caps: how tightly ownership concentration gets restricted, and whether existing large shareholders at major exchanges would need to divest to comply.
A bank-majority stablecoin model, if it survives negotiation, would set a regional precedent that other Asian regulators watching the bill closely could reference when drafting their own rules.
Does South Korea have a stablecoin law today?
South Korea currently has no stablecoin-specific law in force that establishes a dedicated license for stablecoin issuers.
South Korean sentiment toward bank involvement in crypto is not uniformly hostile either.

A recent industry survey covered by shattered.io found that 42% of crypto users actively want their banks to offer crypto-friendly services , a figure that complicates the narrative that bank-led stablecoin control is purely a top-down imposition on an unwilling market.
No introduction date, no vote date, and no effective date have been confirmed.

Exchanges that already operate under the current registration model have generally welcomed the move toward a clearer licensing framework, since a formal license is easier to point to when negotiating with banking partners than a registration certificate under anti-money-laundering rules.
How does this compare to US or EU stablecoin rules?
Two issues remain openly disputed: restrictions on major shareholders’ stakes in crypto exchanges, and who is allowed to issue stablecoins.

The bank-majority model mirrors arguments used in other jurisdictions: a stablecoin backed one-to-one by won deposits is only as trustworthy as the entity holding those deposits, and banks are already licensed, audited, and insured for deposit-taking in ways crypto-native firms are not.

extraction.body: South Korea’s long-awaited Digital Asset Basic Act is entering its final stretch. On October 22, 2026, Lee Eog-weon, chairman of the Financial Services Commission (FSC) , told lawmakers that government consultations on the bill were nearing completion and that officials would push to introduce the legislation as quickly as possible. The bill is still a proposal, not a signed law, but its shape is now public enough to map out what it would change for crypto exchanges, stablecoin issuers, and the software teams that build on top of both. The timing matters. South Korea has one of the most active retail crypto markets in Asia, and its current rules, built around 2021-era reporting requirements for virtual-asset service providers, were never designed for a market with regulated won-stablecoins, bank-led consortia, and AI-driven trading tools. The Digital Asset Basic Act is meant to close that gap. According to a report from Bitcoin Foundation , the bill would cover digital-asset issuance, distribution, disclosure, exchange licensing, and stablecoin issuance in a single framework, replacing the patchwork of guidance exchanges have operated under for years. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The Digital Asset Basic Act is not a single-issue bill. It is a comprehensive rewrite of how South Korea classifies and licenses anything built on blockchain rails. Reports describe its scope as covering four areas at once: how digital assets are issued, how they are distributed and sold to the public, what disclosure obligations issuers face, and how exchanges get licensed to operate. That is a different approach from the 2021 amendments to the Specified Financial Information Act, which mainly forced virtual-asset service providers to register and report suspicious activity to regulators. The new bill goes further by trying to define, in law, what counts as a digital asset and which activities around it require formal authorization. For engineering teams at Korean exchanges, that distinction is not academic. A reporting-only regime lets a platform ship new listing and custody features first and clean up compliance paperwork later. A licensing regime, by contrast, forces legal review into the release cycle for anything touching asset issuance or disclosure. If the Digital Asset Basic Act becomes law with the scope currently described, product and engineering roadmaps at Upbit, Bithumb, and smaller Korean exchanges will need a compliance gate that does not exist today in the same form. Lee Eog-weon has become the public face of the push. Speaking during the current round of government consultations, he said that discussions on the Digital Asset Basic Act were nearing completion and that the government would work to introduce it as soon as possible. He also framed the FSC’s position as a middle path between unchecked expansion and overcaution, telling lawmakers: “We’ve prepared a proposal on how to balance innovation and stability, so we will discuss it together.” That statement, delivered during the 2026 parliamentary audit covered by the Asia Business Daily , is the clearest signal yet that the FSC sees this as a negotiation with the National Assembly rather than a bill it can push through unilaterally. Separate reporting on the FSC’s position, cited by outlets tracking the story, quotes officials saying the agency has already prepared the substantive content of the bill and is now in final-stage consultations before formal introduction. No introduction date, no vote date, and no effective date have been confirmed. Until the National Assembly schedules a reading, the bill remains a proposal. Of everything in the Digital Asset Basic Act, the rules around who can issue a stablecoin have generated the sharpest disagreement. South Korea currently has no stablecoin-specific law in force, meaning there is no dedicated licensing track for a company that wants to issue a won-pegged token today. The bill is meant to create that track, but the fight is over who gets to walk through it. One option on the table, confirmed in multiple reports, would require banks to hold at least 50% plus one share of any stablecoin issuer, giving traditional lenders working control over the entity that mints the token. Supporters argue this keeps stablecoin reserves inside institutions that are already subject to capital and audit requirements. Critics argue it hands an entire emerging product category to the same banks that have historically been slow to build consumer-facing crypto infrastructure. The debate echoes a similar bank-led push covered in shattered.io’s reporting on 21 banks planning a dollar stablecoin consortium , where the same tension between bank control and non-bank competition played out on a different continent. The bank-majority model mirrors arguments used in other jurisdictions: a stablecoin backed one-to-one by won deposits is only as trustworthy as the entity holding those deposits, and banks are already licensed, audited, and insured for deposit-taking in ways crypto-native firms are not. Giving banks a controlling share, in this view, reduces the odds of a reserve mismatch turning into a bank-run-style event for the token. Those two questions, both raised in the same session covered by the Asia Business Daily and relayed by The Block , capture the entire fight in miniature. The FSC has not settled on a final issuer structure, and the 50% plus one proposal remains a disputed policy option rather than enacted law. Not every voice inside South Korea’s financial establishment backs the bank-led model either. Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song told lawmakers during a parliamentary audit that he leans toward allowing private-sector issuance, a position that puts the central bank somewhat at odds with the bank-majority framing the FSC has floated. That split, between the FSC’s proposed compromise and the central bank governor’s own stated preference, is one more sign that the stablecoin-issuer question is not close to settled, regardless of how far along the broader bill is. Stablecoins are not the only sticking point. The bill is also expected to tighten exchange licensing, moving beyond the current registration-and-reporting model toward something closer to a full license regime. That shift would give the FSC more direct authority to approve, suspend, or revoke an exchange’s ability to operate, rather than relying on after-the-fact enforcement against unregistered or non-compliant platforms. It helps to separate what is already true under South Korean law from what the Digital Asset Basic Act would introduce if passed. The table below lays out that split based on reporting from the Financial Services Commission’s public remarks and coverage tracked by regulatory monitors. South Korea did not start regulating crypto in 2026. The country’s current baseline dates to 2021, when amendments to the Specified Financial Information Act required virtual-asset service providers to register with regulators and report suspicious transactions, a framework built mainly to satisfy international anti-money-laundering standards rather than to govern product design or consumer protection in depth. A second wave followed with the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, which focused on custody segregation and market-abuse rules for listed exchanges. The Digital Asset Basic Act is widely described in reporting as the next phase of that sequence, the law meant to cover everything the first two waves left out: issuance frameworks for new tokens, a licensing structure for exchanges that goes beyond registration, and, for the first time, a dedicated path for regulated stablecoins. Each phase has taken longer than the last to negotiate, and this one touches more entrenched interests, banks, exchanges, and non-bank fintechs all have a stake in how the stablecoin-issuer question gets resolved, which helps explain why “final-stage consultations” has not yet turned into a bill number on the National Assembly floor. That last row is not part of the Digital Asset Basic Act itself, but it is running on a parallel legislative track that keeps surfacing in the same hearings. Reports indicate lawmakers and officials are also debating a virtual-asset tax scheduled to take effect in January 2027, with concerns raised about unclear standards and whether exchanges have built the reporting infrastructure in time. That tax debate is a separate bill, but it adds pressure on the same committee calendar that needs to move the Digital Asset Basic Act forward. South Korea is not writing stablecoin and exchange rules in a vacuum. The United States moved first among major economies with a federal stablecoin framework establishing reserve and disclosure requirements for payment-stablecoin issuers. The European Union has run its Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, known as MiCA, since 2024, setting licensing and reserve standards across the bloc. Japan has its own regulated-stablecoin regime under the Payment Services Act, built around licensed trust-company issuance. What sets South Korea’s draft apart, at least as currently described, is the explicit tilt toward bank-majority control of stablecoin issuers. MiCA does not require banks to hold a majority stake in an e-money token issuer, and the US framework likewise allows non-bank entities to issue payment stablecoins under its own chartering and reserve rules. If South Korea’s 50% plus one proposal survives negotiation, it would be a notably more bank-centric model than either of its two largest trading-partner frameworks, a distinction that regulatory trackers such as Chambers and Partners’ South Korea practice guide have flagged as one of the more closely watched open questions in the region’s 2026 regulatory calendar. Industry reaction inside South Korea has split along predictable lines. Exchanges that already operate under the current registration model have generally welcomed the move toward a clearer licensing framework, since a formal license is easier to point to when negotiating with banking partners than a registration certificate under anti-money-laundering rules. Fintechs hoping to issue their own stablecoins have pushed back hardest on the bank-majority proposal, arguing it would hand an entire product category to incumbents before non-bank issuers get a chance to compete. Coverage from the Stablecoin Trade Journal’s review of where Korea’s stablecoin law stands describes the same split, noting that a won-stablecoin framework has reportedly been drafted for final coordination with the broader bill, but with no launch date or authorized issuer determined. That lines up with the FSC’s own framing: the substantive content exists, but it has not cleared the final political hurdles needed to become binding law. Whichever issuer model wins out, reserve attestation will matter, a process shattered.io has walked through separately in a 12-step guide to verifying a stablecoin’s reserves . South Korean sentiment toward bank involvement in crypto is not uniformly hostile either. A recent industry survey covered by shattered.io found that 42% of crypto users actively want their banks to offer crypto-friendly services , a figure that complicates the narrative that bank-led stablecoin control is purely a top-down imposition on an unwilling market. For software teams, the practical impact of the Digital Asset Basic Act will show up less in headline politics and more in integration work. A move from registration-based compliance to a formal licensing regime typically means exchanges have to build and maintain audit trails that satisfy a named regulator’s technical standards, not just internal risk policy. Teams working on exchange APIs, KYC pipelines, and on-chain settlement tooling in South Korea should expect new disclosure fields, stricter identity-verification hooks, and, if the stablecoin provisions pass as described, a defined reserve-attestation interface that bank-majority issuers will need to expose to regulators and, likely, to the public. That is a familiar pattern for engineers who have already built compliance tooling against MiCA’s reserve-reporting requirements in Europe or the reserve-disclosure rules under the US federal stablecoin framework. The specific fields and cadence will differ once South Korea’s bill is finalized, but the shape of the work, instrumenting issuance and redemption flows so a regulator can audit them on demand, is one that fintech engineering teams elsewhere have already had to solve. It is the same category of work covered in shattered.io’s broader software and developer-tooling coverage , and it overlaps heavily with the account-security hardening described in a 12-step guide to crypto exchange account security . Three disputes remain unresolved, and any one of them could push introduction past whatever timeline the FSC is hoping for. First, the stablecoin-issuer structure: whether banks get majority control, a lower minority stake, or a licensing path open to qualified non-bank firms. Second, exchange shareholder caps: how tightly ownership concentration gets restricted, and whether existing large shareholders at major exchanges would need to divest to comply. Third, the overlapping tax debate set for January 2027, which is pulling legislative attention and committee time away from the Digital Asset Basic Act itself. None of these are small technical details. They are the kind of structural questions that, in past legislative sessions, have added months or years to a bill’s path from “final-stage consultations” to an actual vote. The FSC’s own language, as relayed in reporting, stops short of promising a date, saying only that the government will try to introduce the bill as soon as possible once discussions conclude. South Korea’s won is one of the most actively traded fiat currencies against crypto in Asia, and its exchanges process retail volumes that rival much larger markets. The Digital Asset Basic Act is not a single-issue bill. It is a comprehensive rewrite of how South Korea classifies and licenses anything built on blockchain rails. The new bill goes further by trying to define, in law, what counts as a digital asset and which activities around it require formal authorization.

A reporting-only regime lets a platform ship new listing and custody features first and clean up compliance paperwork later. A licensing regime, by contrast, forces legal review into the release cycle for anything touching asset issuance or disclosure. Speaking during the current round of government consultations, he said that discussions on the Digital Asset Basic Act were nearing completion and that the government would work to introduce it as soon as possible. He also framed the FSC’s position as a middle path between unchecked expansion and overcaution, telling lawmakers:
“We’ve prepared a proposal on how to balance innovation and stability, so we will discuss it together.”

That statement, delivered during the 2026 parliamentary audit covered by the Asia Business Daily , is the clearest signal yet that the FSC sees this as a negotiation with the National Assembly rather than a bill it can push through unilaterally. Separate reporting on the FSC’s position, cited by outlets tracking the story, quotes officials saying the agency has already prepared the substantive content of the bill and is now in final-stage consultations before formal introduction. No introduction date, no vote date, and no effective date have been confirmed. Until the National Assembly schedules a reading, the bill remains a proposal.

Supporters argue this keeps stablecoin reserves inside institutions that are already subject to capital and audit requirements. Critics argue it hands an entire emerging product category to the same banks that have historically been slow to build consumer-facing crypto infrastructure. The debate echoes a similar bank-led push covered in shattered.io’s reporting on 21 banks planning a dollar stablecoin consortium , where the same tension between bank control and non-bank competition played out on a different continent.

The bank-majority model mirrors arguments used in other jurisdictions: a stablecoin backed one-to-one by won deposits is only as trustworthy as the entity holding those deposits, and banks are already licensed, audited, and insured for deposit-taking in ways crypto-native firms are not. Giving banks a controlling share, in this view, reduces the odds of a reserve mismatch turning into a bank-run-style event for the token.

The bill is also expected to tighten exchange licensing, moving beyond the current registration-and-reporting model toward something closer to a full license regime. That shift would give the FSC more direct authority to approve, suspend, or revoke an exchange’s ability to operate, rather than relying on after-the-fact enforcement against unregistered or non-compliant platforms.

South Korea did not start regulating crypto in 2026. The country’s current baseline dates to 2021, when amendments to the Specified Financial Information Act required virtual-asset service providers to register with regulators and report suspicious transactions, a framework built mainly to satisfy international anti-money-laundering standards rather than to govern product design or consumer protection in depth. sources.title: South Korea Folds Crypto Into National Asset Law as Japan Passes Its Own Reform
passages: On July 15, 2026 — the same day Japan's parliament formally voted to reclassify cryptocurrencies as financial products — South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance announced the National Asset Basic Act, declaring it would rewrite the legal foundation of how the government manages public wealth, and for the first time in 76 years, digital assets would be part of that foundation.

The announcement makes South Korea the first sovereign asset management statute to embed cryptocurrency inside a sovereign state asset management law — not as a speculative instrument to be taxed and tolerated, but as a category of property the government is legally obligated to manage alongside land, buildings, and intellectual property.

Market Law: A Structural Gap Readers Need to Understand The NABA is only one half of South Korea's digital asset legislative agenda, and understanding the difference between the two halves matters for anyone operating in or watching Korean markets.
South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings.
About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis.

The companion Digital Asset Basic Act — known as the DABA — is the piece that would actually govern how private companies and citizens operate in the crypto market: issuance, trading, custody, supervision, stablecoin licensing, and reserve requirements.
Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko.
Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment.
Officials described the reform as a shift from preservation to value creation: state assets should be actively managed, not merely stored.

The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample.

The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability.

The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments.

extraction.body: On July 15, 2026 — the same day Japan's parliament formally voted to reclassify cryptocurrencies as financial products — South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance announced the National Asset Basic Act, declaring it would rewrite the legal foundation of how the government manages public wealth, and for the first time in 76 years, digital assets would be part of that foundation. The announcement makes South Korea the first sovereign asset management statute to embed cryptocurrency inside a sovereign state asset management law — not as a speculative instrument to be taxed and tolerated, but as a category of property the government is legally obligated to manage alongside land, buildings, and intellectual property. That is a shift in sovereign posture, and it is the kind of shift that historically precedes full institutional market integration. It also happened to coincide, within hours, with Japan's parliament completing its crypto overhaul — the most significant overhaul of its crypto regulatory architecture since the Payment Services Act was written in the aftermath of the Mt. Two G20 democracies, in one trading day, both decided crypto had earned a more permanent address inside the formal financial system. What South Korea's National Asset Basic Act Actually Does The National Asset Basic Act is a management law, not a Bitcoin reserve. The bill, announced at a Presidential Blue House briefing by Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol, would replace the State Property Act of 1950 — legislation written for a postwar economy where government holdings consisted almost entirely of real estate. The current framework was never designed to handle intellectual property, let alone digital assets. Under the proposed act, if the state holds cryptocurrency — through seizure, for instance — it now has a formal legal framework to manage those holdings alongside its other assets, rather than improvising under a statute that does not recognize them. Officials described the reform as a shift from preservation to value creation: state assets should be actively managed, not merely stored. South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings. A joint public-private task force will draft the implementation details and define the scope of covered assets. No detailed implementation rules have been released. The National Asset Basic Act must clear the National Assembly before it takes effect. Market Law: A Structural Gap Readers Need to Understand The NABA is only one half of South Korea's digital asset legislative agenda, and understanding the difference between the two halves matters for anyone operating in or watching Korean markets. The companion Digital Asset Basic Act — known as the DABA — is the piece that would actually govern how private companies and citizens operate in the crypto market: issuance, trading, custody, supervision, stablecoin licensing, and reserve requirements. The DABA categorizes digital assets into "general" and "asset-linked" types, with stablecoins and other instruments pegged to real-world value facing stricter requirements including licensing standards, reserve backing above 100% of circulating supply, and mandatory redemption obligations. It was first proposed in June 2025 to the National Assembly by the ruling Democratic Party. The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability. The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample. The target for passing the DABA remains the second half of 2026, but that timeline depends on resolving a stablecoin dispute still unresolved as of April 2026. Until the DABA clears the National Assembly, South Korea will have a government formally managing virtual assets under statute while the private market waits for its rules. South Korea's Scale in Global Crypto Markets The policy significance of this announcement cannot be separated from the sheer scale of South Korean participation in global digital asset markets. Won-denominated trades have accounted for 30% of all global spot cryptocurrency volume so far in 2026, putting Korea second only to the US dollar market, according to research firm Kaiko. The country's 52 million people generate $26 billion in weekly crypto turnover. About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis. That participation rate is large enough to make crypto policy a central issue in domestic elections. Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko. Upbit and Bithumb dominate Korean trading, handling approximately 96% of all Korean crypto trading volume. Trading volumes fell 21.7% from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026 — from 125.2 trillion won to 98.1 trillion won — as capital rotated away from retail speculation and toward institutional settlement infrastructure, according to CoinGecko data. The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments. Japan Acted the Same Day — and Its Law Is Already Enacted The South Korean announcement did not land in isolation. On the same day, Japan's House of Councillors approved FIEA amendments, formally classifying cryptocurrencies as financial products rather than payment tools — completing passage through both chambers of the Diet. Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment. The FIEA amendments move Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP alongside stocks and bonds under the same legal category as other financial instruments. The new framework introduces several requirements that previously applied only to traditional financial markets: insider trading prohibitions on non-public information, mandatory annual disclosures by token issuers, and substantially harsher penalties for unregistered operators — with maximum prison terms rising from three years to ten years and maximum fines increasing from three million yen to ten million yen.

South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings.
A joint public-private task force will draft the implementation details and define the scope of covered assets.
No detailed implementation rules have been released.
The National Asset Basic Act must clear the National Assembly before it takes effect.

Market Law: A Structural Gap Readers Need to Understand The NABA is only one half of South Korea's digital asset legislative agenda, and understanding the difference between the two halves matters for anyone operating in or watching Korean markets.

The companion Digital Asset Basic Act — known as the DABA — is the piece that would actually govern how private companies and citizens operate in the crypto market: issuance, trading, custody, supervision, stablecoin licensing, and reserve requirements.

The DABA categorizes digital assets into "general" and "asset-linked" types, with stablecoins and other instruments pegged to real-world value facing stricter requirements including licensing standards, reserve backing above 100% of circulating supply, and mandatory redemption obligations.
It was first proposed in June 2025 to the National Assembly by the ruling Democratic Party.

The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability.

The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample.
The target for passing the DABA remains the second half of 2026, but that timeline depends on resolving a stablecoin dispute still unresolved as of April 2026.
Until the DABA clears the National Assembly, South Korea will have a government formally managing virtual assets under statute while the private market waits for its rules.
South Korea's Scale in Global Crypto Markets The policy significance of this announcement cannot be separated from the sheer scale of South Korean participation in global digital asset markets.
Won-denominated trades have accounted for 30% of all global spot cryptocurrency volume so far in 2026, putting Korea second only to the US dollar market, according to research firm Kaiko.
The country's 52 million people generate $26 billion in weekly crypto turnover.
About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis.
That participation rate is large enough to make crypto policy a central issue in domestic elections.
Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko.
Upbit and Bithumb dominate Korean trading, handling approximately 96% of all Korean crypto trading volume.

Trading volumes fell 21.7% from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026 — from 125.2 trillion won to 98.1 trillion won — as capital rotated away from retail speculation and toward institutional settlement infrastructure, according to CoinGecko data.

The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments.
Japan Acted the Same Day — and Its Law Is Already Enacted The South Korean announcement did not land in isolation.

On the same day, Japan's House of Councillors approved FIEA amendments, formally classifying cryptocurrencies as financial products rather than payment tools — completing passage through both chambers of the Diet.
Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment.
The FIEA amendments move Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP alongside stocks and bonds under the same legal category as other financial instruments.

The new framework introduces several requirements that previously applied only to traditional financial markets: insider trading prohibitions on non-public information, mandatory annual disclosures by token issuers, and substantially harsher penalties for unregistered operators — with maximum prison terms rising from three years to ten years and maximum fines increasing from three million yen to ten million yen.

coreStoryFacts.text: South Korea’s long-awaited Digital Asset Basic Act is entering its final stretch.

On October 22, 2026, Lee Eog-weon, chairman of the Financial Services Commission (FSC) , told lawmakers that government consultations on the bill were nearing completion and that officials would push to introduce the legislation as quickly as possible.

The bill is still a proposal, not a signed law, but its shape is now public enough to map out what it would change for crypto exchanges, stablecoin issuers, and the software teams that build on top of both.

South Korea has one of the most active retail crypto markets in Asia, and its current rules, built around 2021-era reporting requirements for virtual-asset service providers, were never designed for a market with regulated won-stablecoins, bank-led consortia, and AI-driven trading tools.

According to a report from Bitcoin Foundation , the bill would cover digital-asset issuance, distribution, disclosure, exchange licensing, and stablecoin issuance in a single framework, replacing the patchwork of guidance exchanges have operated under for years.
South Korea did not start regulating crypto in 2026.
A second wave followed with the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, which focused on custody segregation and market-abuse rules for listed exchanges.

Teams working on exchange APIs, KYC pipelines, and on-chain settlement tooling in South Korea should expect new disclosure fields, stricter identity-verification hooks, and, if the stablecoin provisions pass as described, a defined reserve-attestation interface that bank-majority issuers will need to expose to regulators and, likely, to the public.

That is a familiar pattern for engineers who have already built compliance tooling against MiCA’s reserve-reporting requirements in Europe or the reserve-disclosure rules under the US federal stablecoin framework.

It is the same category of work covered in shattered.io’s broader software and developer-tooling coverage , and it overlaps heavily with the account-security hardening described in a 12-step guide to crypto exchange account security .
It is a comprehensive rewrite of how South Korea classifies and licenses anything built on blockchain rails.
The new bill goes further by trying to define, in law, what counts as a digital asset and which activities around it require formal authorization.

Reports indicate lawmakers and officials are also debating a virtual-asset tax scheduled to take effect in January 2027, with concerns raised about unclear standards and whether exchanges have built the reporting infrastructure in time.
He also framed the FSC’s position as a middle path between unchecked expansion and overcaution, telling lawmakers:

MiCA does not require banks to hold a majority stake in an e-money token issuer, and the US framework likewise allows non-bank entities to issue payment stablecoins under its own chartering and reserve rules.
For engineering teams at Korean exchanges, that distinction is not academic.
A reporting-only regime lets a platform ship new listing and custody features first and clean up compliance paperwork later.
A licensing regime, by contrast, forces legal review into the release cycle for anything touching asset issuance or disclosure.
South Korea is not writing stablecoin and exchange rules in a vacuum.
The European Union has run its Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, known as MiCA, since 2024, setting licensing and reserve standards across the bloc.
Three disputes remain unresolved, and any one of them could push introduction past whatever timeline the FSC is hoping for.
First, the stablecoin-issuer structure: whether banks get majority control, a lower minority stake, or a licensing path open to qualified non-bank firms.
Second, exchange shareholder caps: how tightly ownership concentration gets restricted, and whether existing large shareholders at major exchanges would need to divest to comply.
A bank-majority stablecoin model, if it survives negotiation, would set a regional precedent that other Asian regulators watching the bill closely could reference when drafting their own rules.

extraction.body: South Korea’s long-awaited Digital Asset Basic Act is entering its final stretch. On October 22, 2026, Lee Eog-weon, chairman of the Financial Services Commission (FSC) , told lawmakers that government consultations on the bill were nearing completion and that officials would push to introduce the legislation as quickly as possible. The bill is still a proposal, not a signed law, but its shape is now public enough to map out what it would change for crypto exchanges, stablecoin issuers, and the software teams that build on top of both. The timing matters. South Korea has one of the most active retail crypto markets in Asia, and its current rules, built around 2021-era reporting requirements for virtual-asset service providers, were never designed for a market with regulated won-stablecoins, bank-led consortia, and AI-driven trading tools. The Digital Asset Basic Act is meant to close that gap. According to a report from Bitcoin Foundation , the bill would cover digital-asset issuance, distribution, disclosure, exchange licensing, and stablecoin issuance in a single framework, replacing the patchwork of guidance exchanges have operated under for years. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The Digital Asset Basic Act is not a single-issue bill. It is a comprehensive rewrite of how South Korea classifies and licenses anything built on blockchain rails. Reports describe its scope as covering four areas at once: how digital assets are issued, how they are distributed and sold to the public, what disclosure obligations issuers face, and how exchanges get licensed to operate. That is a different approach from the 2021 amendments to the Specified Financial Information Act, which mainly forced virtual-asset service providers to register and report suspicious activity to regulators. The new bill goes further by trying to define, in law, what counts as a digital asset and which activities around it require formal authorization. For engineering teams at Korean exchanges, that distinction is not academic. A reporting-only regime lets a platform ship new listing and custody features first and clean up compliance paperwork later. A licensing regime, by contrast, forces legal review into the release cycle for anything touching asset issuance or disclosure. If the Digital Asset Basic Act becomes law with the scope currently described, product and engineering roadmaps at Upbit, Bithumb, and smaller Korean exchanges will need a compliance gate that does not exist today in the same form. Lee Eog-weon has become the public face of the push. Speaking during the current round of government consultations, he said that discussions on the Digital Asset Basic Act were nearing completion and that the government would work to introduce it as soon as possible. He also framed the FSC’s position as a middle path between unchecked expansion and overcaution, telling lawmakers: “We’ve prepared a proposal on how to balance innovation and stability, so we will discuss it together.” That statement, delivered during the 2026 parliamentary audit covered by the Asia Business Daily , is the clearest signal yet that the FSC sees this as a negotiation with the National Assembly rather than a bill it can push through unilaterally. Separate reporting on the FSC’s position, cited by outlets tracking the story, quotes officials saying the agency has already prepared the substantive content of the bill and is now in final-stage consultations before formal introduction. No introduction date, no vote date, and no effective date have been confirmed. Until the National Assembly schedules a reading, the bill remains a proposal. Of everything in the Digital Asset Basic Act, the rules around who can issue a stablecoin have generated the sharpest disagreement. South Korea currently has no stablecoin-specific law in force, meaning there is no dedicated licensing track for a company that wants to issue a won-pegged token today. The bill is meant to create that track, but the fight is over who gets to walk through it. One option on the table, confirmed in multiple reports, would require banks to hold at least 50% plus one share of any stablecoin issuer, giving traditional lenders working control over the entity that mints the token. Supporters argue this keeps stablecoin reserves inside institutions that are already subject to capital and audit requirements. Critics argue it hands an entire emerging product category to the same banks that have historically been slow to build consumer-facing crypto infrastructure. The debate echoes a similar bank-led push covered in shattered.io’s reporting on 21 banks planning a dollar stablecoin consortium , where the same tension between bank control and non-bank competition played out on a different continent. The bank-majority model mirrors arguments used in other jurisdictions: a stablecoin backed one-to-one by won deposits is only as trustworthy as the entity holding those deposits, and banks are already licensed, audited, and insured for deposit-taking in ways crypto-native firms are not. Giving banks a controlling share, in this view, reduces the odds of a reserve mismatch turning into a bank-run-style event for the token. Those two questions, both raised in the same session covered by the Asia Business Daily and relayed by The Block , capture the entire fight in miniature. The FSC has not settled on a final issuer structure, and the 50% plus one proposal remains a disputed policy option rather than enacted law. Not every voice inside South Korea’s financial establishment backs the bank-led model either. Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song told lawmakers during a parliamentary audit that he leans toward allowing private-sector issuance, a position that puts the central bank somewhat at odds with the bank-majority framing the FSC has floated. That split, between the FSC’s proposed compromise and the central bank governor’s own stated preference, is one more sign that the stablecoin-issuer question is not close to settled, regardless of how far along the broader bill is. Stablecoins are not the only sticking point. The bill is also expected to tighten exchange licensing, moving beyond the current registration-and-reporting model toward something closer to a full license regime. That shift would give the FSC more direct authority to approve, suspend, or revoke an exchange’s ability to operate, rather than relying on after-the-fact enforcement against unregistered or non-compliant platforms. It helps to separate what is already true under South Korean law from what the Digital Asset Basic Act would introduce if passed. The table below lays out that split based on reporting from the Financial Services Commission’s public remarks and coverage tracked by regulatory monitors. South Korea did not start regulating crypto in 2026. The country’s current baseline dates to 2021, when amendments to the Specified Financial Information Act required virtual-asset service providers to register with regulators and report suspicious transactions, a framework built mainly to satisfy international anti-money-laundering standards rather than to govern product design or consumer protection in depth. A second wave followed with the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, which focused on custody segregation and market-abuse rules for listed exchanges. The Digital Asset Basic Act is widely described in reporting as the next phase of that sequence, the law meant to cover everything the first two waves left out: issuance frameworks for new tokens, a licensing structure for exchanges that goes beyond registration, and, for the first time, a dedicated path for regulated stablecoins. Each phase has taken longer than the last to negotiate, and this one touches more entrenched interests, banks, exchanges, and non-bank fintechs all have a stake in how the stablecoin-issuer question gets resolved, which helps explain why “final-stage consultations” has not yet turned into a bill number on the National Assembly floor. That last row is not part of the Digital Asset Basic Act itself, but it is running on a parallel legislative track that keeps surfacing in the same hearings. Reports indicate lawmakers and officials are also debating a virtual-asset tax scheduled to take effect in January 2027, with concerns raised about unclear standards and whether exchanges have built the reporting infrastructure in time. That tax debate is a separate bill, but it adds pressure on the same committee calendar that needs to move the Digital Asset Basic Act forward. South Korea is not writing stablecoin and exchange rules in a vacuum. The United States moved first among major economies with a federal stablecoin framework establishing reserve and disclosure requirements for payment-stablecoin issuers. The European Union has run its Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, known as MiCA, since 2024, setting licensing and reserve standards across the bloc. Japan has its own regulated-stablecoin regime under the Payment Services Act, built around licensed trust-company issuance. MiCA does not require banks to hold a majority stake in an e-money token issuer, and the US framework likewise allows non-bank entities to issue payment stablecoins under its own chartering and reserve rules. If South Korea’s 50% plus one proposal survives negotiation, it would be a notably more bank-centric model than either of its two largest trading-partner frameworks, a distinction that regulatory trackers such as Chambers and Partners’ South Korea practice guide have flagged as one of the more closely watched open questions in the region’s 2026 regulatory calendar. Exchanges that already operate under the current registration model have generally welcomed the move toward a clearer licensing framework, since a formal license is easier to point to when negotiating with banking partners than a registration certificate under anti-money-laundering rules. Fintechs hoping to issue their own stablecoins have pushed back hardest on the bank-majority proposal, arguing it would hand an entire product category to incumbents before non-bank issuers get a chance to compete. Coverage from the Stablecoin Trade Journal’s review of where Korea’s stablecoin law stands describes the same split, noting that a won-stablecoin framework has reportedly been drafted for final coordination with the broader bill, but with no launch date or authorized issuer determined. That lines up with the FSC’s own framing: the substantive content exists, but it has not cleared the final political hurdles needed to become binding law. Whichever issuer model wins out, reserve attestation will matter, a process shattered.io has walked through separately in a 12-step guide to verifying a stablecoin’s reserves . A recent industry survey covered by shattered.io found that 42% of crypto users actively want their banks to offer crypto-friendly services , a figure that complicates the narrative that bank-led stablecoin control is purely a top-down imposition on an unwilling market. For software teams, the practical impact of the Digital Asset Basic Act will show up less in headline politics and more in integration work. A move from registration-based compliance to a formal licensing regime typically means exchanges have to build and maintain audit trails that satisfy a named regulator’s technical standards, not just internal risk policy. Teams working on exchange APIs, KYC pipelines, and on-chain settlement tooling in South Korea should expect new disclosure fields, stricter identity-verification hooks, and, if the stablecoin provisions pass as described, a defined reserve-attestation interface that bank-majority issuers will need to expose to regulators and, likely, to the public. That is a familiar pattern for engineers who have already built compliance tooling against MiCA’s reserve-reporting requirements in Europe or the reserve-disclosure rules under the US federal stablecoin framework. The specific fields and cadence will differ once South Korea’s bill is finalized, but the shape of the work, instrumenting issuance and redemption flows so a regulator can audit them on demand, is one that fintech engineering teams elsewhere have already had to solve. It is the same category of work covered in shattered.io’s broader software and developer-tooling coverage , and it overlaps heavily with the account-security hardening described in a 12-step guide to crypto exchange account security . Three disputes remain unresolved, and any one of them could push introduction past whatever timeline the FSC is hoping for. First, the stablecoin-issuer structure: whether banks get majority control, a lower minority stake, or a licensing path open to qualified non-bank firms. Second, exchange shareholder caps: how tightly ownership concentration gets restricted, and whether existing large shareholders at major exchanges would need to divest to comply. Third, the overlapping tax debate set for January 2027, which is pulling legislative attention and committee time away from the Digital Asset Basic Act itself. None of these are small technical details. The new bill goes further by trying to define, in law, what counts as a digital asset and which activities around it require formal authorization.

A reporting-only regime lets a platform ship new listing and custody features first and clean up compliance paperwork later. A licensing regime, by contrast, forces legal review into the release cycle for anything touching asset issuance or disclosure. Speaking during the current round of government consultations, he said that discussions on the Digital Asset Basic Act were nearing completion and that the government would work to introduce it as soon as possible. He also framed the FSC’s position as a middle path between unchecked expansion and overcaution, telling lawmakers:
“We’ve prepared a proposal on how to balance innovation and stability, so we will discuss it together.”

That statement, delivered during the 2026 parliamentary audit covered by the Asia Business Daily , is the clearest signal yet that the FSC sees this as a negotiation with the National Assembly rather than a bill it can push through unilaterally. Separate reporting on the FSC’s position, cited by outlets tracking the story, quotes officials saying the agency has already prepared the substantive content of the bill and is now in final-stage consultations before formal introduction. No introduction date, no vote date, and no effective date have been confirmed. Until the National Assembly schedules a reading, the bill remains a proposal.

Critics argue it hands an entire emerging product category to the same banks that have historically been slow to build consumer-facing crypto infrastructure. The debate echoes a similar bank-led push covered in shattered.io’s reporting on 21 banks planning a dollar stablecoin consortium , where the same tension between bank control and non-bank competition played out on a different continent.

The bank-majority model mirrors arguments used in other jurisdictions: a stablecoin backed one-to-one by won deposits is only as trustworthy as the entity holding those deposits, and banks are already licensed, audited, and insured for deposit-taking in ways crypto-native firms are not. Giving banks a controlling share, in this view, reduces the odds of a reserve mismatch turning into a bank-run-style event for the token.

Stablecoins are not the only sticking point. The bill is also expected to tighten exchange licensing, moving beyond the current registration-and-reporting model toward something closer to a full license regime. That shift would give the FSC more direct authority to approve, suspend, or revoke an exchange’s ability to operate, rather than relying on after-the-fact enforcement against unregistered or non-compliant platforms.

passages: On July 15, 2026 — the same day Japan's parliament formally voted to reclassify cryptocurrencies as financial products — South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance announced the National Asset Basic Act, declaring it would rewrite the legal foundation of how the government manages public wealth, and for the first time in 76 years, digital assets would be part of that foundation.

The announcement makes South Korea the first sovereign asset management statute to embed cryptocurrency inside a sovereign state asset management law — not as a speculative instrument to be taxed and tolerated, but as a category of property the government is legally obligated to manage alongside land, buildings, and intellectual property.

Market Law: A Structural Gap Readers Need to Understand The NABA is only one half of South Korea's digital asset legislative agenda, and understanding the difference between the two halves matters for anyone operating in or watching Korean markets.
South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings.
About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis.

The companion Digital Asset Basic Act — known as the DABA — is the piece that would actually govern how private companies and citizens operate in the crypto market: issuance, trading, custody, supervision, stablecoin licensing, and reserve requirements.
Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko.
Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment.
Officials described the reform as a shift from preservation to value creation: state assets should be actively managed, not merely stored.

The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample.

The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability.

The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments.

extraction.body: On July 15, 2026 — the same day Japan's parliament formally voted to reclassify cryptocurrencies as financial products — South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance announced the National Asset Basic Act, declaring it would rewrite the legal foundation of how the government manages public wealth, and for the first time in 76 years, digital assets would be part of that foundation. The announcement makes South Korea the first sovereign asset management statute to embed cryptocurrency inside a sovereign state asset management law — not as a speculative instrument to be taxed and tolerated, but as a category of property the government is legally obligated to manage alongside land, buildings, and intellectual property. That is a shift in sovereign posture, and it is the kind of shift that historically precedes full institutional market integration. It also happened to coincide, within hours, with Japan's parliament completing its crypto overhaul — the most significant overhaul of its crypto regulatory architecture since the Payment Services Act was written in the aftermath of the Mt. Two G20 democracies, in one trading day, both decided crypto had earned a more permanent address inside the formal financial system. What South Korea's National Asset Basic Act Actually Does The National Asset Basic Act is a management law, not a Bitcoin reserve. The bill, announced at a Presidential Blue House briefing by Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol, would replace the State Property Act of 1950 — legislation written for a postwar economy where government holdings consisted almost entirely of real estate. The current framework was never designed to handle intellectual property, let alone digital assets. Under the proposed act, if the state holds cryptocurrency — through seizure, for instance — it now has a formal legal framework to manage those holdings alongside its other assets, rather than improvising under a statute that does not recognize them. Officials described the reform as a shift from preservation to value creation: state assets should be actively managed, not merely stored. South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings. A joint public-private task force will draft the implementation details and define the scope of covered assets. No detailed implementation rules have been released. The National Asset Basic Act must clear the National Assembly before it takes effect. Market Law: A Structural Gap Readers Need to Understand The NABA is only one half of South Korea's digital asset legislative agenda, and understanding the difference between the two halves matters for anyone operating in or watching Korean markets. The companion Digital Asset Basic Act — known as the DABA — is the piece that would actually govern how private companies and citizens operate in the crypto market: issuance, trading, custody, supervision, stablecoin licensing, and reserve requirements. The DABA categorizes digital assets into "general" and "asset-linked" types, with stablecoins and other instruments pegged to real-world value facing stricter requirements including licensing standards, reserve backing above 100% of circulating supply, and mandatory redemption obligations. It was first proposed in June 2025 to the National Assembly by the ruling Democratic Party. The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability. The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample. The target for passing the DABA remains the second half of 2026, but that timeline depends on resolving a stablecoin dispute still unresolved as of April 2026. Until the DABA clears the National Assembly, South Korea will have a government formally managing virtual assets under statute while the private market waits for its rules. South Korea's Scale in Global Crypto Markets The policy significance of this announcement cannot be separated from the sheer scale of South Korean participation in global digital asset markets. Won-denominated trades have accounted for 30% of all global spot cryptocurrency volume so far in 2026, putting Korea second only to the US dollar market, according to research firm Kaiko. The country's 52 million people generate $26 billion in weekly crypto turnover. About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis. That participation rate is large enough to make crypto policy a central issue in domestic elections. Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko. Upbit and Bithumb dominate Korean trading, handling approximately 96% of all Korean crypto trading volume. Trading volumes fell 21.7% from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026 — from 125.2 trillion won to 98.1 trillion won — as capital rotated away from retail speculation and toward institutional settlement infrastructure, according to CoinGecko data. The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments. Japan Acted the Same Day — and Its Law Is Already Enacted The South Korean announcement did not land in isolation. On the same day, Japan's House of Councillors approved FIEA amendments, formally classifying cryptocurrencies as financial products rather than payment tools — completing passage through both chambers of the Diet. Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment. The FIEA amendments move Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP alongside stocks and bonds under the same legal category as other financial instruments. The new framework introduces several requirements that previously applied only to traditional financial markets: insider trading prohibitions on non-public information, mandatory annual disclosures by token issuers, and substantially harsher penalties for unregistered operators — with maximum prison terms rising from three years to ten years and maximum fines increasing from three million yen to ten million yen.

The current framework was never designed to handle intellectual property, let alone digital assets.

Under the proposed act, if the state holds cryptocurrency — through seizure, for instance — it now has a formal legal framework to manage those holdings alongside its other assets, rather than improvising under a statute that does not recognize them.
Officials described the reform as a shift from preservation to value creation: state assets should be actively managed, not merely stored.
South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings.
A joint public-private task force will draft the implementation details and define the scope of covered assets.
No detailed implementation rules have been released.
The National Asset Basic Act must clear the National Assembly before it takes effect.

Market Law: A Structural Gap Readers Need to Understand The NABA is only one half of South Korea's digital asset legislative agenda, and understanding the difference between the two halves matters for anyone operating in or watching Korean markets.

The companion Digital Asset Basic Act — known as the DABA — is the piece that would actually govern how private companies and citizens operate in the crypto market: issuance, trading, custody, supervision, stablecoin licensing, and reserve requirements.

The DABA categorizes digital assets into "general" and "asset-linked" types, with stablecoins and other instruments pegged to real-world value facing stricter requirements including licensing standards, reserve backing above 100% of circulating supply, and mandatory redemption obligations.
It was first proposed in June 2025 to the National Assembly by the ruling Democratic Party.

The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability.

The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample.
The target for passing the DABA remains the second half of 2026, but that timeline depends on resolving a stablecoin dispute still unresolved as of April 2026.
Until the DABA clears the National Assembly, South Korea will have a government formally managing virtual assets under statute while the private market waits for its rules.
South Korea's Scale in Global Crypto Markets The policy significance of this announcement cannot be separated from the sheer scale of South Korean participation in global digital asset markets.
Won-denominated trades have accounted for 30% of all global spot cryptocurrency volume so far in 2026, putting Korea second only to the US dollar market, according to research firm Kaiko.
The country's 52 million people generate $26 billion in weekly crypto turnover.
About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis.
That participation rate is large enough to make crypto policy a central issue in domestic elections.
Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko.
Upbit and Bithumb dominate Korean trading, handling approximately 96% of all Korean crypto trading volume.

Trading volumes fell 21.7% from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026 — from 125.2 trillion won to 98.1 trillion won — as capital rotated away from retail speculation and toward institutional settlement infrastructure, according to CoinGecko data.

The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments.
Japan Acted the Same Day — and Its Law Is Already Enacted The South Korean announcement did not land in isolation.

On the same day, Japan's House of Councillors approved FIEA amendments, formally classifying cryptocurrencies as financial products rather than payment tools — completing passage through both chambers of the Diet.
Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment.
The FIEA amendments move Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP alongside stocks and bonds under the same legal category as other financial instruments.

The new framework introduces several requirements that previously applied only to traditional financial markets: insider trading prohibitions on non-public information, mandatory annual disclosures by token issuers, and substantially harsher penalties for unregistered operators — with maximum prison terms rising from three years to ten years and maximum fines increasing from three million yen to ten million yen.

extraction.body: OpenAI's ChatGPT application launched in November 2022 and amassed 100 million users within just a couple of months, marking the beginning of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Since then, many stocks in the semiconductor, cloud computing, and even software industries have delivered blistering returns, leading the broader market higher. But volatility is on the rise as investors question the sustainability of the AI infrastructure spending boom. Practically every stock in the AI sphere is pulling back, including some of the highest-quality names: Corrections are a normal part of the investing journey, but investors who want to limit their exposure to extreme volatility might want to consider buying an exchange-traded fund (ETF) like the iShares Future AI and Tech ETF ( ARTY -4.63% ) . It holds a portfolio of 50 leading AI stocks, so it saves investors from having to pick winners and losers. Read on. The iShares Future AI and Tech ETF aims to give investors exposure to the entire AI value chain, which includes infrastructure, software, and services. Below are a couple of its most noteworthy holdings from each of those categories. Some of the other noteworthy AI stocks in the iShares ETF include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing , Broadcom , Micron Technology , and Space Exploration Technologies . The iShares Future AI and Tech ETF was originally created in 2018 with a focus on AI and robotics, but it was restructured in August 2024 to narrow its mandate to AI alone. As a result, it doesn't have a very long track record of performance for investors to analyze. However, investors should never park all of their money into an ETF that only focuses on one area of the stock market. Concerns are mounting about the sustainability of the AI spending boom as funding gets harder to come by , particularly at favorable terms. Even the best companies are feeling the effects, with Anthropic now expected to go public at a valuation of $1.5 trillion, down from initial expectations of $2 trillion. If these challenges persist, the iShares ETF could suffer a sharp correction. Cost is another consideration. The iShares ETF has an expense ratio of 0.47%, which translates to an annual fee of $47 for every $10,000 invested. That doesn't sound like much at face value, but it's roughly 15 times more than an investor would pay in a passive index fund offered by Vanguard , for example, which can cost as little as 0.03% per year. The iShares ETF's higher fees relate to its actively managed portfolio. Rather than simply tracking an index, a team of professionals will regularly buy and sell stocks based on what they believe will deliver the best returns. This can yield great results, but it also costs more money. In summary, the iShares Future AI and Tech ETF might be the perfect addition to a diversified portfolio that doesn't already have much exposure to the AI industry, but it definitely shouldn't be an investor's only position.
