This decline follows a peak of $2,788 within the same timeframe, driven by selling pressure.

Many traders are closely monitoring the $2,300 mark because ETH has dipped toward it twice in October and bounced back each time. The lowest point during this sell-off was $2,313, and holders are eager to see if Ether can stay above $2,300. If that level breaks, it raises concerns about how far the price could fall.
Ether trades 51.4% below its all-time high, meaning it would need to nearly double to return to that peak. In 2026 alone, ETH has dropped about 19.0% from its December 31, 2025, price of $2,967.
By comparison, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has lost only 3.8% over the same period, suggesting Ether has declined about five times as much and continues to lose ground against the larger cryptocurrency.

A moving average reflects the average closing price over a specific number of days, so being below both averages means buyers from the past 50 days are losing money. Often, these buyers may sell during any price rally to reclaim their investments, turning these averages into resistance levels where selling pressure increases.
Despite the October drops, Ether is still benefiting from a summer rally, having gained approximately 29.2% over the last 90 days, rising from $1,860 on July 24.

In the sell-off on October 15, ETH hit a low of $2,313 but managed to close the day at $2,439. On October 18, it dipped again to $2,325, then recovered to close at $2,408. Buyers quickly stepped in both times.

The lowest daily close in the past month came on October 17, when ETH settled at $2,400, leaving the price just $3 above. However, ETH hasn't tested support below $2,313 in the last month, so the closest prior reference point is $1,860 from July 24, about 22.6% lower than the current price.

A spot Ether ETF holds Ethereum and trades like a stock, so its flows reflect traditional investors' actions. On October 21, U.S. spot Ether ETFs saw an inflow of $15 million, following outflows of $26.1 million on October 20 and $103.3 million on October 19.

Throughout most of the sell-off, investors pulled money from these funds. The largest one-day outflow recorded was $201.9 million on October 6. The next day, ETH opened at $2,697 but closed at $2,573, a 4.6% drop.

By October 21, cumulative net inflows—representing the total money added since the funds launched—fell to $12.8 billion from $14.0 billion on September 28. Additionally, total net assets declined from $17.9 billion to $15.4 billion since September 22. A single day of inflows seems too minor to reverse this downward trend.
Bitmine Immersion Technologies ( NYSE:BMNR ) has staked another 159,728 ETH, valued at $390.6 million, bringing its total staked Ether to 5.23 million, worth around $12.8 billion.

Staking involves locking up ETH to secure the Ethereum network, allowing holders to earn rewards. Since staked coins are not immediately accessible, this helps reduce the supply available for sale during market panic, which may support prices around $2,300.

Bitmine has also continued to buy ETH during this downturn. Its holdings increased from 6.02 million ETH, as of an October 5 announcement, to 6.04 million by October 19, equivalent to about $14.5 billion at the $2,403 price point. However, this persistent buying has not been enough to outweigh selling pressure from ETFs.

I believe ETH is likely to hold above $2,300 on its next test. Buyers have defended this level twice in October, there were positive ETF flows on October 21, and Bitmine continues to take coins off the market. However, a rebound to the 30-day high of $2,788—about 16.1% higher—could be much more challenging. For this to happen, ETH needs consistent daily closes above $2,313, clear both moving averages, and see steady ETF inflows.

If the support breaks, the consequences could be significant. A daily close below $2,313, especially if ETF outflows exceed $100 million again, as seen on October 14 and October 19, would challenge this outlook. ETH has no tested support below that level in the past month, which could set it on a path toward $1,860—around 22.6% lower than the current price. Conversely, a close above $2,520 would confirm a positive bounce.

passages: Buyers have stepped in to defend a key Ethereum price floor twice this month, but ETF outflows and a 12% monthly slide are testing their resolve. Whether that support holds or shatters could determine if ETH revisits levels not seen…

Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) trades around $2,400, about $100 above the critical $2,300 support level that buyers successfully defended twice in October 2026. As of October 22, 2026, the Ethereum price is approximately $2,403, marking a 2.3% decline in 24 hours and a 12.6% drop over the past 30 days. This decline follows a peak of $2,788 within the same timeframe, driven by selling pressure.

Many traders are closely monitoring the $2,300 mark because ETH has dipped toward it twice in October and bounced back each time. The lowest point during this sell-off was $2,313, and holders are eager to see if Ether can stay above $2,300. If that level breaks, it raises concerns about how far the price could fall.
Ether trades 51.4% below its all-time high , meaning it would need to nearly double to return to that peak. In 2026 alone, ETH has dropped about 19.0% from its December 31, 2025, price of $2,967.
By comparison, Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) has lost only 3.8% over the same period, suggesting Ether has declined about five times as much and continues to lose ground against the larger cryptocurrency.

ETH is also below its 20-day moving average of $2,520 and the 50-day moving average of $2,551. A moving average reflects the average closing price over a specific number of days, so being below both averages means buyers from the past 50 days are losing money. Often, these buyers may sell during any price rally to reclaim their investments, turning these averages into resistance levels where selling pressure increases.
Despite the October drops, Ether is still benefiting from a summer rally, having gained approximately 29.2% over the last 90 days, rising from $1,860 on July 24.

In the sell-off on October 15 , ETH hit a low of $2,313 but managed to close the day at $2,439. On October 18, it dipped again to $2,325, then recovered to close at $2,408. Buyers quickly stepped in both times.

The lowest daily close in the past month came on October 17, when ETH settled at $2,400, leaving the price just $3 above. However, ETH hasn’t tested support below $2,313 in the last month, so the closest prior reference point is $1,860 from July 24, about 22.6% lower than the current price.

A spot Ether ETF holds Ethereum and trades like a stock, so its flows reflect traditional investors’ actions. On October 21, U.S. spot Ether ETFs saw an inflow of $15 million, following outflows of $26.1 million on October 20 and $103.3 million on October 19.

Throughout most of the sell-off, investors pulled money from these funds. The largest one-day outflow recorded was $201.9 million on October 6. The next day, ETH opened at $2,697 but closed at $2,573, a 4.6% drop.

By October 21, cumulative net inflows—representing the total money added since the funds launched—fell to $12.8 billion from $14.0 billion on September 28. Additionally, total net assets declined from $17.9 billion to $15.4 billion since September 22. A single day of inflows seems too minor to reverse this downward trend.

Bitmine Immersion Technologies ( NYSE:BMNR | BMNR Price Prediction ) has staked another 159,728 ETH, valued at $390.6 million, bringing its total staked Ether to 5.23 million, worth around $12.8 billion.

Staking involves locking up ETH to secure the Ethereum network, allowing holders to earn rewards. Since staked coins are not immediately accessible, this helps reduce the supply available for sale during market panic, which may support prices around $2,300.

Bitmine has also continued to buy ETH during this downturn. Its holdings increased from 6.02 million ETH, as of an October 5 announcement, to 6.04 million by October 19, equivalent to about $14.5 billion at the $2,403 price point. However, this persistent buying has not been enough to outweigh selling pressure from ETFs.

I believe ETH is likely to hold above $2,300 on its next test. Buyers have defended this level twice in October, there were positive ETF flows on October 21, and Bitmine continues to take coins off the market. However, a rebound to the 30-day high of $2,788—about 16.1% higher—could be much more challenging. For this to happen, ETH needs consistent daily closes above $2,313, clear both moving averages, and see steady ETF inflows.

If the support breaks, the consequences could be significant. A daily close below $2,313, especially if ETF outflows exceed $100 million again, as seen on October 14 and October 19, would challenge this outlook. ETH has no tested support below that level in the past month, which could set it on a path toward $1,860—around 22.6% lower than the current price. Conversely, a close above $2,520 would confirm a positive bounce.

The company has an important economic moat in reusable rockets, which have made it much less expensive to launch payloads into orbit. That edge helped SpaceX build Starlink, the world's largest satellite internet service. CEO Elon Musk wants to combine those proficiencies to build orbital (space-based) data centers, which could theoretically solve the power and cooling challenges associated with terrestrial data centers. extraction.body: Nvidia ( NVDA -3.85% ) is one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies in the world, but is the semiconductor specialist as good at picking AI stocks as it is at building GPUs? Nvidia's public equity portfolio includes several companies that are capitalizing on the AI boom, and three of them, Space Exploration Technologies ( SPCX -5.47% ) , CoreWeave ( CRWV -8.27% ) , and Intel ( INTC -5.79% ) , make up almost 88% of the portfolio. Are these AI stocks retail investors should also consider buying? SpaceX conducted the largest IPO in history in June. The company is best-known for revolutionizing the space travel industry. But its biggest opportunities are in the AI sector, or at least, that's what the company itself believes. SpaceX's CEO, Elon Musk, recently said that within five years, AI will account for the overwhelming majority of the company's value. SpaceX is projecting $1 trillion in revenue by 2030, a substantial portion of which will presumably come from AI. Now, there are some reasons to be bullish on SpaceX's AI business. During the company's second quarter, AI revenue was $2.6 billion, up 247.5% compared to the year-ago period. The rocket company's total revenue was $7.8 billion, up 92% year over year. So, AI is growing much faster than the rest of the business, and SpaceX is doubling down and investing significant sums into this segment. The company also has deals (to provide AI computing capacity) with some important names, including Alphabet ( GOOG -2.12% ) ( GOOGL -2.14% ) and Anthropic . However, the market has already factored in some of SpaceX's AI-related success in its share price: The company is worth nearly $2 trillion despite generating significantly less revenue than similarly sized peers and remaining unprofitable. Further, it will face significant competition in the field and may not capture a large enough market share (and the total market may be smaller than expected) in the AI industry . There is little room for error for SpaceX. Investors should wait for a much better entry point to initiate a position. CoreWeave recently posted excellent second-quarter results. The company's revenue of $2.6 billion rose 112.5% compared to the year-ago period. CoreWeave remains unprofitable, with its operating and net losses widening compared to the prior-year quarter. But CoreWeave is investing heavily into building data centers tailored to AI, and it is paying off -- it ended the period with a cloud backlog of $104 billion, which soared by 245.5% year over year. CoreWeave's trailing-12-month revenue is only $7.6 billion. The company's revenue backlog provides significant visibility into the next few quarters, during which we should see the top line continue to expand rapidly. Meanwhile, the stock doesn't seem overvalued. CoreWeave isn't profitable, but its price-to-sales ratio of 7.2 is reasonable given how quickly the top line is growing and the fact that it should maintain that pace for the foreseeable future, based on its backlog. There are some risks. For instance, CoreWeave relies heavily on a single customer for the majority of its revenue, probably Microsoft ( MSFT -1.29% ) . Even with that caveat, though, the company looks likely to deliver competitive returns over the next few years. Intel, a leader in the CPU (Central Processing Unit) market, is also posting solid results. In the second quarter, the company's revenue increased by 25% year over year to $16.1 billion, while its adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.42, up from the $0.10 adjusted loss per share reported in the year-ago period. Intel is seeing soaring demand for its products thanks to the rise of agentic AI, or self-directed systems that can help companies automate tasks and boost productivity by autonomously working toward goals. AI agents run on CPUs -- that's where Intel shines. And the company may ride this tailwind over the next few years. Is the stock still attractive at current levels, after more than doubling this year? My view is that, in Wall Street parlance, Intel is a "hold" rather than a strong "buy." Here are three reasons why. First, Intel has lost some ground to its biggest competitor in the CPU space, Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD -6.96% ) , in recent quarters. Second, Intel has encountered manufacturing issues that it has yet to fully resolve. Finally, the company seems somewhat overvalued. It is trading at 80.7x forward earnings -- versus an average of 21.7x for information technology stocks. Intel might grow its earnings fast enough over the next few years to justify its valuation, given its position in the CPU market and the rising demand for its hardware. However, investors who don't currently have a stake in the company should wait for a pullback. Prosper Junior Bakiny has positions in Alphabet and Nvidia. So, AI is growing much faster than the rest of the business, and SpaceX is doubling down and investing significant sums into this segment.

The company also has deals (to provide AI computing capacity) with some important names, including Alphabet ( GOOG -2.12% ) ( GOOGL -2.14% ) and Anthropic . However, the market has already factored in some of SpaceX's AI-related success in its share price: The company is worth nearly $2 trillion despite generating significantly less revenue than similarly sized peers and remaining unprofitable.

Further, it will face significant competition in the field and may not capture a large enough market share (and the total market may be smaller than expected) in the AI industry . There is little room for error for SpaceX. Investors should wait for a much better entry point to initiate a position.

CoreWeave recently posted excellent second-quarter results. The company's revenue of $2.6 billion rose 112.5% compared to the year-ago period. CoreWeave remains unprofitable, with its operating and net losses widening compared to the prior-year quarter. But CoreWeave is investing heavily into building data centers tailored to AI, and it is paying off -- it ended the period with a cloud backlog of $104 billion, which soared by 245.5% year over year. CoreWeave's trailing-12-month revenue is only $7.6 billion.

The company's revenue backlog provides significant visibility into the next few quarters, during which we should see the top line continue to expand rapidly. Meanwhile, the stock doesn't seem overvalued. CoreWeave isn't profitable, but its price-to-sales ratio of 7.2 is reasonable given how quickly the top line is growing and the fact that it should maintain that pace for the foreseeable future, based on its backlog. There are some risks. For instance, CoreWeave relies heavily on a single customer for the majority of its revenue, probably Microsoft ( MSFT -1.29% ) . Even with that caveat, though, the company looks likely to deliver competitive returns over the next few years.

Intel, a leader in the CPU (Central Processing Unit) market, is also posting solid results. In the second quarter, the company's revenue increased by 25% year over year to $16.1 billion, while its adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.42, up from the $0.10 adjusted loss per share reported in the year-ago period. Intel is seeing soaring demand for its products thanks to the rise of agentic AI, or self-directed systems that can help companies automate tasks and boost productivity by autonomously working toward goals.

AI agents run on CPUs -- that's where Intel shines. And the company may ride this tailwind over the next few years. Is the stock still attractive at current levels, after more than doubling this year? My view is that, in Wall Street parlance, Intel is a "hold" rather than a strong "buy." Here are three reasons why.

First, Intel has lost some ground to its biggest competitor in the CPU space, Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD -6.96% ) , in recent quarters. Second, Intel has encountered manufacturing issues that it has yet to fully resolve. Finally, the company seems somewhat overvalued. It is trading at 80.7x forward earnings -- versus an average of 21.7x for information technology stocks.

Intel might grow its earnings fast enough over the next few years to justify its valuation, given its position in the CPU market and the rising demand for its hardware. However, investors who don't currently have a stake in the company should wait for a pullback.

extraction.body: The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet. The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems. The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks. The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible. The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk. Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore , the United Kingdom , Australia , Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems. Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure. Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches. OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure. The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals. Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates. The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses. passages: The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.

The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.

The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.

The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.

Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore , the United Kingdom , Australia , Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems.

Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.

Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.

OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.

The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. passages: Microsoft is closing down The Garage, a set of popular maker spaces where employees worked on experimental projects and collaborated on surprising new apps and hardware during the company’s annual hackathon events.
Microsoft is now planning to wind down its Garage locations, and some spaces will be closed as soon as tomorrow, Friday, October 23rd.
Microsoft’s fixes for Windows 11 have made it “up to 20 percent more responsive,” according to the company.

The main Garage space was located at Microsoft’s Redmond, Washington, campus and served as the central hub for around 15 Garage locations across the US, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia.

“This system is storefront-agnostic, meaning you benefit even when playing games purchased on Steam, as long as the Xbox PC app is installed on your PC,” says Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes. * Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump’s ballroom.

extraction.body: Microsoft is closing down The Garage, a set of popular maker spaces where employees worked on experimental projects and collaborated on surprising new apps and hardware during the company’s annual hackathon events. “We’re winding down The Garage program as a centralized function,” says Microsoft in an internal FAQ to employees, seen by Notepad. “We will continue to explore new ways to help employees build skills, collaborate across boundaries, and bring a hacker mindset to their work.” GeekWire first reported on The Garage’s closure. The main Garage space was located at Microsoft’s Redmond, Washington, campus and served as the central hub for around 15 Garage locations across the US, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. Microsoft employees could use it to experiment with prototypes, build hardware, and even turn hobbies into full Microsoft products. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella regularly attended Garage hackathons, giving employees a chance to showcase their projects and attract the attention of senior executives. Many apps and services have emerged from The Garage over its 17-year history, including the AI-powered Seeing AI app that describes objects and text to people who are blind or have low vision. It was born out of a 2015 hackathon event and shipped 10 years ago. Microsoft employee Tuong Do used The Garage to develop Mouse Without Borders in his spare time, working on it during evenings and weekends. Microsoft employees have also used The Garage to develop new learning tools and accessibility features for Word, Microsoft Edge, and PowerPoint. I would point you to the Microsoft Garage hall of fame for a list of all the top projects, but Microsoft has removed the website — erasing the rich history of its employee-led workshop. One of the most famous success stories of The Garage was Microsoft’s Xbox Adaptive Controller. The accessibility-focused Xbox controller was a collective effort by employees across Xbox and Surface, but it originated at a hackathon event where employees were experimenting with building a gaming device that used Kinect motion-sensing technology to track movements and translate them to an Xbox controller. While the device was nearly cut due to budget constraints, it eventually launched and went on to become the star of Microsoft’s 2019 Super Bowl commercial. Microsoft is now planning to wind down its Garage locations, and some spaces will be closed as soon as tomorrow, Friday, October 23rd. The closure of The Garage will also mean changes to Microsoft’s annual employee hackathon event, which could potentially disappear. We’ll have more to share at a later date,” says Microsoft’s internal FAQ. Internally, the company is trying to sell employees on the idea that “the spirit of experimentation that once lived primarily in dedicated programs is now reflected in how teams work every day.” Employees I’ve spoken to see the closure as the latest in Microsoft’s continued cutbacks. Earlier this year Microsoft closed its employee library and cut back on subscriptions in favor of an “AI-powered learning experience.” The library used to house thousands of books, journals, and reports that employees could use to learn, research, and explore ideas — much like The Garage. “We’re grateful to the employees, volunteers, and partners who helped build The Garage and look forward to continuing its legacy in new forms,” says Microsoft’s FAQ. It’s hard to imagine anything replicating the unique mix of expert advisers, dedicated maker spaces, hands-on workshops, and internship programs that The Garage offered employees looking to develop new skills. The pad * Microsoft employee causes an Xbox AI stir. Microsoft employee Brandon Stirrup posted multiple times on X this week to get everyone talking about AI use in gaming. “Gaming is the only industry where leaders are afraid to talk about AI,” said Stirrup. We’re using AI.” Stirrup’s posts elicited the usual response from gamers against AI, but he said he’s “happy to take the hit if it means hundreds at Xbox can stop pretending that they’re not using AI.” Hours after Stirrup’s posts, he disabled his X account. * Microsoft’s new Photos app combines your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud galleries. Microsoft has redesigned its Photos app for Windows 11, combining images and videos from your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud into a single space. The viewer has also been sped up, with improved HDR viewing and better file type support. * Microsoft says Windows 11 is now “more responsive” and runs better on 8GB of RAM. Microsoft’s fixes for Windows 11 have made it “up to 20 percent more responsive,” according to the company. Microsoft has made improvements to Start, File Explorer, Search, Edge, and other parts of Windows 11 to make the OS feel faster. A big part of the improvements comes down to better memory management, to the point where there is now a “meaningful difference” on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. The new nine-piece “Yxstaby” collection from Ikea was designed in collaboration with Microsoft. Nvidia has rolled out a new GPU driver (621.01) this week that enables Microsoft’s new Advanced Shader Delivery technology to speed up game launches. The technology also removes mid-game “just-in-time” shader compilation, reducing stuttering and CPU spikes. Microsoft’s Advanced Shader Delivery works by offloading shader compilation for different hardware combinations to the cloud. “This system is storefront-agnostic, meaning you benefit even when playing games purchased on Steam, as long as the Xbox PC app is installed on your PC,” says Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes. * Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump’s ballroom. Microsoft donated $10 million, which puts it roughly in the middle set of tech donations from the likes of Apple ($25 million), Amazon ($5 million), Nvidia ($25 million), Google ($22 million), and Meta ($5 million). * Xbox mandates a four-day return to office.

The main Garage space was located at Microsoft’s Redmond, Washington, campus and served as the central hub for around 15 Garage locations across the US, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. Microsoft employees could use it to experiment with prototypes, build hardware, and even turn hobbies into full Microsoft products. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella regularly attended Garage hackathons, giving employees a chance to showcase their projects and attract the attention of senior executives. It was born out of a 2015 hackathon event and shipped 10 years ago. Microsoft employee Tuong Do used The Garage to develop Mouse Without Borders in his spare time, working on it during evenings and weekends. Microsoft employees have also used The Garage to develop new learning tools and accessibility features for Word, Microsoft Edge, and PowerPoint. One of the most famous success stories of The Garage was Microsoft’s Xbox Adaptive Controller. sources.title: Spotify confirms Family Plan crackdown, but calls it a ‘routine improvement’
passages: Spotify confirmed the reports of its crackdown on Family Plan sharing during its third-quarter call with investors, calling its new method “a routine improvement” to its existing verification tools.

Over the past several days, reports had surfaced indicating that Spotify was rolling out a “QR code verification” method, where the app would prompt members on its Family Plan to verify they lived with the plan manager by scanning a QR code.

The move is meant to boost subscriptions to Spotify’s profitable Premium plans, rather than allowing adult children or friends who live apart from gaming the system to get a cheaper plan by splitting a Family Plan subscription.
“Family Plan has existed for a long while.

It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base,” said Norström “As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have.
There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it.
As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time,” he added.

The executive said that the company’s attempt to better verify its users is not something that would have an end date or would ever be complete, but would be considered an ongoing routine improvement.
Plan members have seven days to complete the QR code after getting a notification, which means they could be out of luck if they live outside the home and aren’t planning a return visit anytime soon.
If the verification window is missed, they won’t be able to join another Family or Duo plan for 12 months, but would instead have to shift to an individual plan that they pay for themselves.

Organizations building AI agents face a common challenge: Every request, whether a routine status check or complex analysis, typically gets routed to a single large, expensive model. This one-size-fits-all approach can drive up API costs, introduce unpredictable latency, and remove the possibility of offline operation. Even routine queries that could resolve locally end up requiring a full network round-trip to a cloud-hosted large language model (LLM). The Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework (AAIF), built with Strands Agents, takes a different approach. Instead of routing all requests to a single large model, AAIF uses small language models (SLMs) to handle routine tasks locally. More complex requests are routed to cloud-hosted models through Amazon Bedrock . This approach builds on the research position from Belcak et al. at NVIDIA . They argue that small language models are “sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable, and necessarily more economical for many invocations in agentic systems.” Built on Strands Agents, the framework demonstrates how intelligent model orchestration can help reduce costs while maintaining low latency for local operations. In this post, we walk through the key components of AAIF using Strands Agents with local SLMs through Ollama and cloud models through Amazon Bedrock. We use an Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring scenario as a reference implementation. AAIF organizes AI processing into three layers, each optimized for different task types, as Figure 1 shows: Figure 1: The three AAIF processing layers for smart orchestration, local processing, and cloud processing Figure 1 shows the complete AAIF system architecture. At the center sits the Strands agent, which connects to an Ollama runtime hosting both the 1B-parameter orchestrator model and the vision model. The agent exposes three tools: get_device_telemetry for local sensor data retrieval, analyze_camera_feed for on-device vision processing through llama3.2-vision, and get_expert_insights which calls Amazon Bedrock through boto3 for complex analysis. Incoming user requests flow through the SLM orchestrator, which classifies each request and dispatches it to either a local tool or the cloud endpoint based on task complexity. Figure 2: Complete AAIF system architecture showing the Strands agent, Ollama runtime, tool integrations, and Amazon Bedrock connectivity The framework adapts to your deployment constraints rather than requiring you to restructure your infrastructure around it. This architecture runs on edge devices like a Raspberry Pi with 8 GB of memory, in full cloud deployments where all inference hits Amazon Bedrock, or in hybrid configurations that combine local speed with cloud reasoning. The flexibility comes from separating the routing logic (the SLM orchestrator) from the processing tools, which you can swap or reconfigure independently depending on available hardware and network connectivity. For this walkthrough, you should have the following prerequisites: Create a file called aaif_agent.py and add the following components. Strands Agents uses the @tool decorator to define capabilities that agents can invoke. Start by creating tools for local processing. The first tool retrieves device telemetry data. In a production environment, this would connect to actual IoT sensors. For this walkthrough, it uses simulated device data: The second tool performs vision analysis using a local SLM. The llama3.2-vision model runs entirely on local hardware, which means sensitive camera feeds don’t leave the device: For complex analysis that requires broader reasoning, create a tool that calls Amazon Bedrock. This tool is invoked only when the orchestrator determines that local models can’t handle the request: The core of AAIF is the Strands agent configuration. The agent uses a local SLM (llama3.2:1b) as its orchestrator. Strands Agents supports multiple model providers, and here we use the Ollama provider to run the orchestrator locally: The SLM-powered orchestrator analyzes each request and routes it to the appropriate tool without hardcoded keyword matching. The routing happens through the model’s understanding of the request: Table 1: Request, routing, and latency estimates for local compared to cloud inference With the agent configured, you can interact with it directly: The agent automatically classifies each request and routes it to the appropriate processing layer. No explicit routing rules are needed. The AAIF architecture adapts to different infrastructure requirements by changing the model configuration: When your workload runs entirely in the cloud and no edge hardware is available, replace the Ollama model configuration with Amazon Bedrock for all processing. This routes every request through managed cloud inference, giving you auto scaling without requiring local GPU resources. Teams with reliable low-latency connectivity and no data residency constraints benefit most from this configuration: The hybrid configuration keeps the local SLM orchestrator intact while adding cloud models for requests that exceed local model capabilities. This is the default AAIF configuration shown in this walkthrough. It suits environments where most requests are routine enough to resolve locally, but some require the broader reasoning of a larger model. Cost savings can come from the roughly 80 percent of traffic that doesn’t hit a paid API endpoint. For environments that are fully air-gapped or have strict data sovereignty requirements, replace the cloud tool with a larger local model and run all processing on-device. A 3B-parameter model running on hardware with adequate memory can handle moderately complex tasks that the 1B orchestrator would otherwise escalate. The trade-off is reduced reasoning depth on the hardest queries, but the benefit is data not leaving the premises: The implementation in this post uses local tool calls defined directly in the agent code. For production deployments with multiple agents sharing tools across services, expose these tools as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. MCP provides a standardized interface for tool discovery and invocation, so you can centralize tool management and reuse tools across different agents and environments. In Figure 3, we show how to convert AAIF tools into MCP servers for distributed, centralized tool calling. In the distributed configuration as shown in Figure 3, Device 1 acts as the orchestrating hub, running the Strands agent with the SLM router and a local telemetry tool. It connects through the MCP protocol to Device 2, which runs an edge vision processing server with llama3.2-vision. Device 3 serves as a cloud analytics gateway connected to Amazon Bedrock. From the orchestrator’s perspective, all remote tools appear as local function calls because the MCP transport layer handles serialization and network communication transparently. Figure 3: Distributed intelligence with MCP servers To avoid incurring future charges, complete the following cleanup steps: We showed how to build cost-effective AI agents using the Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework with Strands Agents. By routing routine requests to local SLMs and reserving cloud models on Amazon Bedrock for complex analysis, AAIF can help reduce API costs while maintaining low latency for routine operations. Before you run this pattern in production, add responsible AI controls to the cloud inference path, since those requests carry tool outputs, retrieved data, and user input. You can attach Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to the Strands BedrockModel with a guardrail ID and version. It then applies content filters for harmful categories, prompt injection filters, and contextual grounding checks that block responses not supported by the source data. To apply the same policies to the local SLM tier, call the standalone ApplyGuardrail API on its inputs and outputs. This way, every request follows one safety standard no matter which model handles it. This architectural pattern applies beyond IoT monitoring. A healthcare organization could run patient monitoring locally while routing diagnosis support to cloud models. A financial services firm could process transactions on-premises and reserve cloud capacity for risk analysis. A manufacturing team could run quality control vision models at the edge while sending optimization requests to the cloud. Even routine queries that could resolve locally end up requiring a full network round-trip to a cloud-hosted large language model (LLM).

The Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework (AAIF), built with Strands Agents, takes a different approach. Instead of routing all requests to a single large model, AAIF uses small language models (SLMs) to handle routine tasks locally. More complex requests are routed to cloud-hosted models through Amazon Bedrock . This approach builds on the research position from Belcak et al. at NVIDIA . They argue that small language models are “sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable, and necessarily more economical for many invocations in agentic systems.” Built on Strands Agents, the framework demonstrates how intelligent model orchestration can help reduce costs while maintaining low latency for local operations.

In this post, we walk through the key components of AAIF using Strands Agents with local SLMs through Ollama and cloud models through Amazon Bedrock. We use an Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring scenario as a reference implementation.
AAIF organizes AI processing into three layers, each optimized for different task types, as Figure 1 shows:
Figure 1: The three AAIF processing layers for smart orchestration, local processing, and cloud processing

Figure 1 shows the complete AAIF system architecture. At the center sits the Strands agent, which connects to an Ollama runtime hosting both the 1B-parameter orchestrator model and the vision model. The agent exposes three tools: get_device_telemetry for local sensor data retrieval, analyze_camera_feed for on-device vision processing through llama3.2-vision, and get_expert_insights which calls Amazon Bedrock through boto3 for complex analysis. Incoming user requests flow through the SLM orchestrator, which classifies each request and dispatches it to either a local tool or the cloud endpoint based on task complexity.
Figure 2: Complete AAIF system architecture showing the Strands agent, Ollama runtime, tool integrations, and Amazon Bedrock connectivity

The framework adapts to your deployment constraints rather than requiring you to restructure your infrastructure around it. This architecture runs on edge devices like a Raspberry Pi with 8 GB of memory, in full cloud deployments where all inference hits Amazon Bedrock, or in hybrid configurations that combine local speed with cloud reasoning. The flexibility comes from separating the routing logic (the SLM orchestrator) from the processing tools, which you can swap or reconfigure independently depending on available hardware and network connectivity.
For this walkthrough, you should have the following prerequisites:
Create a file called aaif_agent.py and add the following components.
Strands Agents uses the @tool decorator to define capabilities that agents can invoke. Start by creating tools for local processing.
The first tool retrieves device telemetry data. In a production environment, this would connect to actual IoT sensors. For this walkthrough, it uses simulated device data:
The second tool performs vision analysis using a local SLM. The llama3.2-vision model runs entirely on local hardware, which means sensitive camera feeds don’t leave the device:
For complex analysis that requires broader reasoning, create a tool that calls Amazon Bedrock. This tool is invoked only when the orchestrator determines that local models can’t handle the request:

The core of AAIF is the Strands agent configuration. The agent uses a local SLM (llama3.2:1b) as its orchestrator. Strands Agents supports multiple model providers, and here we use the Ollama provider to run the orchestrator locally:
The SLM-powered orchestrator analyzes each request and routes it to the appropriate tool without hardcoded keyword matching. The routing happens through the model’s understanding of the request:
Table 1: Request, routing, and latency estimates for local compared to cloud inference
With the agent configured, you can interact with it directly:
The agent automatically classifies each request and routes it to the appropriate processing layer. No explicit routing rules are needed.
The AAIF architecture adapts to different infrastructure requirements by changing the model configuration:

When your workload runs entirely in the cloud and no edge hardware is available, replace the Ollama model configuration with Amazon Bedrock for all processing. This routes every request through managed cloud inference, giving you auto scaling without requiring local GPU resources. Teams with reliable low-latency connectivity and no data residency constraints benefit most from this configuration:

The hybrid configuration keeps the local SLM orchestrator intact while adding cloud models for requests that exceed local model capabilities. This is the default AAIF configuration shown in this walkthrough. It suits environments where most requests are routine enough to resolve locally, but some require the broader reasoning of a larger model. Cost savings can come from the roughly 80 percent of traffic that doesn’t hit a paid API endpoint.

For environments that are fully air-gapped or have strict data sovereignty requirements, replace the cloud tool with a larger local model and run all processing on-device. A 3B-parameter model running on hardware with adequate memory can handle moderately complex tasks that the 1B orchestrator would otherwise escalate. The trade-off is reduced reasoning depth on the hardest queries, but the benefit is data not leaving the premises:

The implementation in this post uses local tool calls defined directly in the agent code. For production deployments with multiple agents sharing tools across services, expose these tools as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. MCP provides a standardized interface for tool discovery and invocation, so you can centralize tool management and reuse tools across different agents and environments. In Figure 3, we show how to convert AAIF tools into MCP servers for distributed, centralized tool calling.

In the distributed configuration as shown in Figure 3, Device 1 acts as the orchestrating hub, running the Strands agent with the SLM router and a local telemetry tool. It connects through the MCP protocol to Device 2, which runs an edge vision processing server with llama3.2-vision. Device 3 serves as a cloud analytics gateway connected to Amazon Bedrock. From the orchestrator’s perspective, all remote tools appear as local function calls because the MCP transport layer handles serialization and network communication transparently.
Figure 3: Distributed intelligence with MCP servers

We showed how to build cost-effective AI agents using the Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework with Strands Agents. By routing routine requests to local SLMs and reserving cloud models on Amazon Bedrock for complex analysis, AAIF can help reduce API costs while maintaining low latency for routine operations.

Before you run this pattern in production, add responsible AI controls to the cloud inference path, since those requests carry tool outputs, retrieved data, and user input. You can attach Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to the Strands BedrockModel with a guardrail ID and version. It then applies content filters for harmful categories, prompt injection filters, and contextual grounding checks that block responses not supported by the source data. To apply the same policies to the local SLM tier, call the standalone ApplyGuardrail API on its inputs and outputs. This way, every request follows one safety standard no matter which model handles it.

This architectural pattern applies beyond IoT monitoring. A healthcare organization could run patient monitoring locally while routing diagnosis support to cloud models.
